Dividend.title: Alaska: Dividend (State)
Dividend.subtitle: Permanent Fund Dividend and the state budget

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: The Permanent Fund Dividend (PFD) is the yearly cash payment every eligible Alaskan receives from the earnings of the state's oil wealth fund. With Governor Mike Dunleavy barred by term limits, the size of the dividend is the central fiscal question in the open race for governor.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: The 2026 dividend is $1,200, combining $1,000 and a $200 energy relief payment, at a cost of more than $800 million. The amount has not followed the statutory formula since 2016, and the fund now pays for between 50 and 60% of state operations in an ordinary year.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Democrats. Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, the only Democrat on the ballot, says a $4,000 payout would drain the fund within decades. He backs a smaller, sustainable dividend inside a balanced budget.

Republicans. Bernadette Wilson, the top Republican in the primary, wants the dividend set by the statutory formula and attacks his past support for a state income tax.

Voters. The payment has helped reduce poverty for decades, so its size is felt directly in household budgets.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: Voters will rank four candidates, one Democrat and three Republicans. Wilson has urged rival Republicans to quit, arguing a split field helps Kreiss-Tomkins. The winner will shape whether Alaska turns to new revenue or deeper cuts.

Energy.title: Alaska: Energy (State)
Energy.subtitle: Railbelt power and the Cook Inlet gas shortfall

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: Southcentral Alaska relies on Cook Inlet natural gas to heat homes and generate most Railbelt electricity, and that basin is in decline. The risk of a winter shortage makes energy supply and cost a test for the next governor.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: The Railbelt grid serves more than 75% of Alaskans, and a state forecast found Cook Inlet demand could outpace supply as soon as 2027. In August, the Anchorage Daily News warned the region could enter this winter short of gas during a sustained cold snap, after Enstar drew on stored gas more heavily than ever.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Democrats. Kreiss-Tomkins backs a broad strategy that uses every energy source and has floated a statewide energy bond.

Republicans. Wilson and Treg Taylor call the North Slope gas line the biggest lever on costs and prefer market driven, deregulatory fixes.

Public debate. Policymakers have long resisted imports, calling them discordant for a state with gas still in the ground, yet imported LNG now looks likely in the medium term.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: Energy is a pocketbook issue across the Railbelt, home to most Alaska voters. Because every candidate backs more Cook Inlet drilling and the gas line, the contest turns on credibility and financing. Any shortage this winter would land at once on the new governor.

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: Alaska hosts major Army, Air Force and missile defence sites near Russia and the Arctic. The Golden Dome missile shield, launched by President Trump, has raised the state's profile, and defence spending is a centrepiece of Senator Sullivan's campaign.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: The final FY 2026 defence bill authorises more than $292 million for Alaska military construction, including $80 million for Army barracks at Fort Wainwright. Fort Greely holds about 80 interceptors, and the bill tracks $115 million to reopen the Adak Island installation.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Republicans. Sullivan wrote the GOLDEN DOME Act, much of it now in the defence bill, and calls Alaska the cornerstone of homeland missile defence. Republicans also tout new Alaska military spending secured at his urging.

Democrats. Peltola runs on an Alaska First message and has sought to distinguish her campaign from the national party, avoiding a direct clash on defence.

Voters. Polling has centred on the cost of living, with Peltola's campaign saying frustration over costs drives her support.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: Defence spending is one of Sullivan's strongest arguments in a toss up race. It lets him campaign on delivery for Alaska rather than on national politics. Peltola's task is to match his credibility on security while keeping the race focused on local costs.

Mining.title: Alaska: Mining (Fed)
Mining.subtitle: Ambler Road, Pebble and federal land decisions

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: Federal permits decide whether Alaska's large mineral deposits are developed. The Trump administration revived the Ambler Road to a copper district in Northwest Alaska, while the Pebble prospect near Bristol Bay remains contested, putting mining squarely into the Senate race.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: In October 2025, President Trump ordered agencies to reissue Ambler Road permits and announced a $35.6 million federal investment in Trilogy Metals for about a 10% stake. The industrial road would run 211 miles, and the Trilogy venture is targeting mine permit submissions in 2026. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum has floated federal investment in the road itself.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Republicans. Senator Sullivan supports Ambler Road and the Donlin gold mine but opposes Pebble.

Democrats. Mary Peltola backs only the regulatory advancement of Donlin and Ambler, so communities can decide, and also opposes Pebble.

Voters. Environmental groups and Indigenous communities warn the road would cut across the Western Arctic Caribou Herd's migration path and damage subsistence lifestyles.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: Mining tests Peltola's standing with rural Alaska Native voters, whose regional corporations have long shaped her positions, against Sullivan's development record. With both major forecasters rating the race a toss up, small shifts in rural turnout matter.

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: Alaska LNG would carry North Slope gas to Southcentral Alaska and later to an export terminal at Nikiski. Developer Glenfarne owns 75% and the state owns 25% through the Alaska Gasline Development Corporation.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: Phase One is a 739 mile, 42 inch pipeline for Alaskan users. In May, Glenfarne said all major North Slope producers had committed enough gas for a Phase One final investment decision, once expected by the end of 2025. That decision still looms, and first gas is targeted for 2029.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Both parties. All four governor candidates back the $44.5 to $54.5 billion line but split on how to pay for it.

Republicans. Wilson and Taylor favour market driven, deregulatory approaches, and Wilson promises a permitting shot clock.

Democrats. Kreiss-Tomkins has floated a statewide energy bond and has not ruled out higher oil and gas taxes.

Voters. Years of delay feed doubt, with some calling the line a pipe dream.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html:
The line is the main jobs promise in the governor's race, so visible progress helps whoever claims it.

India and U.S. interests. India's GAIL has held initial talks to buy Alaska LNG as New Delhi raises U.S. energy imports to narrow its trade surplus. Delays to the export phase would slow that potential supply route.

Voting.title: Alaska: Voting (State)
Voting.subtitle: Ballot Measure 2 and ranked choice voting

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: Alaska elects candidates through open top four primaries and ranked choice general elections, adopted by voters in 2020. Ballot Measure 2 would repeal both, restore closed primaries and scrap some campaign disclosure rules.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: A similar repeal failed in 2024 by 737 votes out of 320,985 cast. In April, President Trump urged Alaskans to repeal the system, naming Senator Dan Sullivan and Representative Nick Begich among the repeal's backers. Maine is the only other state using ranked choice voting in regular statewide elections.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Republicans. State party leaders made repeal a top goal after 2024, and the Repeal Now campaign calls the system confusing and burdensome.

Opponents. Unions and Alaska Native organisations back the campaign against repeal. Opponents argue the system gives voters more choice and deters extreme partisans.

Voters. Some voters report confusion, yet ballot error rates have remained very low.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: The measure shares the ballot with a Senate race in which one poll has Mary Peltola leading Sullivan 50% to 48% after ranked choice tallies. Repeal would not change this year's count but would reset the rules for future elections. Motivated voters on both sides of the measure could tip a Senate race decided by a few points.

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: Arizona voters wrote abortion rights into the constitution in 2024. The fight has moved to the courts and legislature, and the governor's veto is now the main barrier to new limits.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: Proposition 139 passed with 61.61% of the vote, protecting abortion until fetal viability. In February 2026, Judge Gregory Como struck down the 24 hour waiting period, the ban on telemedicine abortions and the ban on abortions sought over genetic abnormalities. Republican legislative leaders have appealed. Lawmakers still advanced 11 of 16 bills that experts say could conflict with the amendment.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Democrats. Hobbs has vetoed fetal personhood bills and similar measures. She warns, "Under my watch, we are not going to go backwards."

Republicans. Biggs calls himself pro life and has cosponsored federal legislation that would amount to a national ban. His adviser did not directly say whether he would back repealing Proposition 139.

Attorney General. Democrat Kris Mayes declined to defend the old laws and called their defeat a "major victory." Senate President Warren Petersen, her Republican challenger, leads the chamber pursuing the appeal.

Advocates. Reproductive Freedom for All plans a $23.5 million national "My Body, My Ballot" campaign.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: Abortion helps explain Hobbs' strength with women, who back her 56.7% to 28.8%. Mayes leads Petersen by 15 points.

Water.title: Arizona: Water (Mixed)
Water.subtitle: Colorado River cuts and state groundwater rules

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: Arizona carries the largest share of new federal Colorado River cuts, while its groundwater rules remain contested. The next governor manages the state response and will represent Arizona in the 2028 river talks.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: Interior Department guidelines set Lower Basin cuts of 1.25 million acre feet a year in 2027 and 2028. Under the states' proposed sharing deal, Arizona takes 760,000, California 440,000 and Nevada 50,000. The rules took effect on 1 October, with Arizona's cuts official from 1 January 2027, and Nevada has sued.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Democrats. Governor Katie Hobbs ties conservation to Arizona's bargaining power and says, "I am not interested in relaxing our state's groundwater protection." She cancelled Fondomonte's land leases, halting its pumping.

Republicans. Andy Biggs wants more supply, not new rules, saying, "We've got a massive supply of groundwater." He would revive the Yuma Desalting Plant, built in 1992 and used only twice.

Rural voters. Both sides back a rural groundwater framework but split over how much pumping to allow. Biggs' running mate Sine Kerr blocked rural limits as Senate water chair.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: Water gives Biggs a line of attack on Hobbs' river diplomacy. HighGround put Hobbs ahead 49.5% to 34.3% in August and by 17 points in October. The deal still needs legislative approval.

Defense.title: California: Defense (Fed)
Defense.subtitle: Defence spending, industry and troop deployments

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: Southern California is enjoying a defence technology boom built on federal budgets. At the same time, the federal deployment of the state's National Guard in Los Angeles turned military power into a domestic political fight.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: President Trump's latest budget seeks a record $1.5 trillion for the military. Los Angeles County companies won $15 billion in defence contracts last year,. In San Diego, military spending supported about 357,000 jobs in 2025, down more than 16,000 from 2024. A federal judge ruled in September 2025 that the Los Angeles Guard deployment violated the Posse Comitatus Act.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Trump administration. It defended the deployment, and an appeals panel found it "likely that the President lawfully exercised his statutory authority." President Trump ended the Los Angeles deployment on 31 December 2025.

Democrats. Some congressional Democrats resist higher defence budgets, yet Ted Lieu's 36th District gained more than $3.3 billion in contracts from 2015 to 2025. Maxine Waters backed a bill to abolish the Space Force.

Critics. Lindsay Koshgarian of the National Priorities Project says, "we are maybe seeing the limits of that now."

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: The contract boom is concentrated in heavily Democratic Los Angeles County. That leaves Democrats balancing local aerospace jobs against national calls to cut Pentagon spending.

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: California holds a far larger share of the nation's homeless population than of its residents. After years of heavy spending, the debate has shifted from how much the state spends to what the money achieves.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: Nearly a quarter of homeless U.S. residents live in California, which has about 11% of the population. A 2024 state audit found California spent about $24 billion over five years without consistently tracking outcomes. The main local grant, HHAP, received no new money for 2025 to 2026 and $500 million for 2026 to 2027, half its earlier $1 billion. Governor Gavin Newsom says the number sleeping outside fell 9% last year, a claim his critics dispute.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Democrats. Becerra gives Newsom an A on effort but promises accountability for money sent to cities, saying "results are what you see on the streets." In the debate he pledged, "We will make sure the encampments are cleared."

Republicans. Hilton calls housing first a "complete disaster", wants camping laws enforced and would overhaul HHAP funding.

Local governments. Counties and cities warned that halving HHAP "will stop progress in its tracks."

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: Homelessness is Hilton's sharpest attack on the Democratic record, which he calls an "absolute scandal" that "shames our state." Becerra's risk is owning Newsom's results while promising stricter oversight.

Housing.title: California: Housing (Mixed)
Housing.subtitle: Housing costs, state zoning and federal housing funds

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: Housing costs sit at the core of California's affordability crisis. The state controls zoning and permits, while federal grants shape support for low income and homeless housing.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: Voters will decide Proposition 1, an $11.25 billion bond expected to fund up to 40,000 rental units and help about 40,000 households buy homes. Federally, HUD tried to cap permanent housing at 30% of about $4 billion in Continuum of Care grants until a judge blocked the shift in July 2026.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Democrats. Xavier Becerra would declare the shortage a state emergency, expand SB 79 transit zoning and hold cities to their targets. California YIMBY endorsed him after he backed a 90 day permit deadline.

Republicans. Steve Hilton wants 10 new cities built where counties opt in, limits on CEQA lawsuits and a $50,000 cap on fees for new single family homes. He wants to "stop forcing apartment buildings into suburban areas."

Trump administration. HUD says "Housing First has failed" and is moving 2026 funding toward recovery and self sufficiency.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: Housing anchors the cost of living message both candidates run on. Becerra led 55% to 37% in the August UC Berkeley IGS and Los Angeles Times poll. Proposition 1 will test whether voters still trust state borrowing to fix supply.

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: Los Angeles became the testing ground for the Trump administration's new at large arrest strategy in June 2025. Enforcement has surged again ahead of the midterms, putting California's sanctuary law at the centre of the governor's race.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: Researchers found nearly 15,000 people arrested in the Los Angeles ICE region were deported between January 2025 and May 2026. At the June 2025 peak, arrests of people with no criminal conviction were more than 3,400% above 2024 levels. After DHS announced a surge in sanctuary cities on 26 September, at least 45 people were arrested across Southern California in a single week in October.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Democrats. Becerra defends the SB 54 sanctuary law, arguing the federal government "can not tell us in California to do federal immigration enforcement."

Republicans. Hilton backs cooperating with ICE "100 percent" and "totally disagrees" with SB 54, yet in the debate said he wants to "lower the temperature" and focus on "dangerous criminals."

Flashpoint. Becerra told Hilton, "You seem to welcome immigrants who look like you, but deport immigrants who look like me." Hilton called it "disgraceful."

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: Becerra frames the contest as a vote on President Trump, who endorsed Hilton. Enforcement also shapes House races such as the 22nd District, where Valadao faces Democrat Randy Villegas.

Insurance.title: California: Insurance (Fed)
Insurance.subtitle: Home insurance and the federal backstop debate

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: California's home insurance market is shrinking as insurers retreat from fire prone areas. The state regulates rates, but federal reinsurance and forest bills have brought Congress into the debate.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: Insurers did not renew more than 2.8 million homeowners policies in fire prone ZIP codes from 2020 to 2025. Enrolment in the FAIR Plan, the insurer of last resort, rose 43% from September 2024 to December 2025, and its insured exposure grew from about $50 billion in 2018 to $458 billion in 2024. The Fix Our Forests Act passed the House 279 to 141 but has no Senate floor vote scheduled.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Democrats. Senator Adam Schiff's INSURE Act would create a federal catastrophe reinsurance programme in the Treasury. He warns "the most valuable property a family may own is becoming uninsurable."

Bipartisan. Senator Alex Padilla joined Republicans John Curtis and Tim Sheehy to introduce the Senate forests bill.

Industry. The insurers' trade group APCIA says, "We cannot afford to remain trapped in a cycle of disaster and recovery."

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: With federal bills stalled, insurance remains a state problem in practice. That raises the stakes of the insurance commissioner race between Democrats Jane Kim and Ben Allen. Kim proposes a state run disaster insurance programme that critics say could cost tens of billions to launch.

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: The 2025 federal tax and spending law, H.R. 1, cuts Medicaid funding and adds work requirements. California must decide how much of the gap it can fill.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: H.R. 1 reduces federal Medicaid funding by about $1 trillion over a decade. About 4.8 million Medi-Cal adults fall under work requirements from 1 January 2027, and the state estimates 1.1 million will lose coverage by 2029 to 2030. UCLA researchers project up to 2.98 million fewer enrollees by 2028, a figure that includes the state's own freeze on new undocumented adult enrolment.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Republicans. Valadao voted for H.R. 1, calling work requirements for nondisabled adults reasonable and saying "Sustainable means taking care of those who need it most."

Democrats. Villegas accuses Valadao of voting "to cut healthcare for nearly 70,000 people in the Valley" and pledges to reverse the cuts.

Governor's race. Becerra, a former U.S. health secretary, says eligible immigrant families should not be scared away from care. Hilton says "everyone should have access to health care" but notes other states cover immigrants more narrowly.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: Medicaid is the defining issue in the 22nd District, which had a 64% Medicaid enrolment rate in 2024, the highest of any Republican held seat. The new boundaries only partly overlap the old seat.

Redistricting.title: California: Redistricting (State)
Redistricting.subtitle: Proposition 50 and the new House map

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: In 2025 California voters approved new congressional maps drawn by the Democratic legislature. The maps replace those of the independent commission until after the 2030 census and reshape the state's 2026 House races.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: Proposition 50 passed with 64.42% of the vote. The map targets five Republican held seats, and flipping all five could leave Republicans with four of 52. A federal panel upheld it 2 to 1, and the U.S. Supreme Court denied the state Republican Party's emergency appeal on 4 February 2026 without comment or dissent.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Republicans. The map forced incumbents to adapt. Ken Calvert and Young Kim now face each other in the 40th District, Darrell Issa retired and Kevin Kiley left the party to run as an independent in the 6th.

Democrats. They hold the edge in the 48th, rated Leans Democratic, where Marni von Wilpert faces Republican Jim Desmond.

Litigants. Hilton sued to block the measure, but a judge denied an injunction before the vote.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: Valadao's 22nd District, rated competitive, is the main remaining test of the new map. A September SurveyUSA poll gave Democrats a 58% to 33% lead on the statewide House ballot. Democrats won 63.83% of the June primary House vote.

Restoration.title: California: Restoration (Fed)
Restoration.subtitle: Federal aid for Los Angeles wildfire recovery

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: The January 2025 Los Angeles fires destroyed more than 16,000 structures. Twenty one months on, rebuilding depends on federal money that has not arrived, making recovery a test of federal and state relations.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: Newsom has cut his aid request to $15.7 billion, down from $33 billion, but President Trump has not sent Congress a disaster request for the fires. California has filed more than $1.5 billion in FEMA reimbursement claims, of which FEMA has obligated $37 million, about 2.5%. About 1,400 households are set to lose disaster case managers at the end of October in a funding standoff with FEMA.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Democrats. Becerra calls winning $30 billion in federal disaster money "job one" and promises to "fight, fight and fight." Representative Judy Chu says the case management gap "risks abandoning survivors."

Republicans. The White House says it has obligated billions for recovery and that California mismanaged the crisis. Hilton blames local permitting, where "you can't get the permit until you get your insurance."

Survivors. "The safety net has been pulled out from under me," says survivor Mary Landau.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: The aid gap lets Becerra run against Washington and a Republican Congress. Hilton instead argues the delays are a failure of state and city government, mocking Newsom's promised "Marshall Plan" for Los Angeles.

Water.title: California: Water (State)
Water.subtitle: Water supply, storage and the Delta tunnel

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: Water divides California by region, pitting Central Valley farms and southern cities against Delta communities and environmental limits. The governor oversees the State Water Project and its largest proposed upgrade, the Delta tunnel.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: The State Water Project runs 705 miles of aqueducts and canals serving about two thirds of Californians and Central Valley farmland. Newsom's bid to fast track the $20 billion Delta tunnel stalled in the Legislature again in September 2025.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Republicans. Hilton opposes the tunnel as "ridiculous, and unnecessary." He backs Sites, desalination and the Trump administration's plan to raise Shasta Dam, and says groundwater rules should be "cut back and shut down wherever possible."

Democrats. Becerra has no firm tunnel position, saying "we should never say no to anything until we've examined it completely." As attorney general he sued the first Trump administration more than 120 times, including over water deliveries.

Delta opponents. Critics call the tunnel "the zombie offspring of the zombie project," while supporters say "the need is urgent."

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: Water matters most in the Central Valley, home to the competitive 22nd District held by Republican David Valadao. Becerra declined interviews on water and has no detailed water plan on his website, ceding the policy detail to Hilton.

Wildfire.title: California: Wildfire (State)
Wildfire.subtitle: Wildfire prevention, utilities and emergency response

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: Wildfire risk shapes California's budget, power bills and emergency planning. After the 2025 Los Angeles fires, the state moved to shore up its utility wildfire fund, while voters question its readiness for the next disaster.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: Newsom signed SB 254 on 19 September 2025. It creates an $18 billion continuation account for the utility Wildfire Fund, half from extending an existing charge on customer bills and half from shareholders. Utilities will also fund $6 billion in prevention work, including undergrounding lines. The January 2025 fires destroyed more than 16,000 structures, and delayed alerts drew criticism.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Democrats. Becerra would fund buffer zones and home hardening, build a working statewide alert system and keep crews ready all year without routine 60 to 70 hour weeks. "It's not a matter of if; it's a matter of when," he says.

Republicans. Hilton attacks the state's recovery record, describing burnt buildings with "nothing happening" and shifting bureaucratic rules at permit offices.

Ratepayers. CalChamber says SB 254 "does not raise utility customer rates," though the fund relies on extending an existing bill charge.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: Wildfire is a competence test for the next governor. Becerra met Altadena fire survivors in September, while Hilton ties recovery to his critique of state bureaucracy.

Energy.title: Colorado: Energy (State)
Energy.subtitle: Utility bills and data centre demand

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: Rising electricity and gas bills have made energy a cost of living issue in Colorado. Fast growing data centre demand adds pressure, and state regulators and the next governor will decide who pays.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: Xcel Energy asked to raise electric rates by nearly 10% in 2026, about $9.94 a month for a typical home. Pending requests would push gas bills up 11.4% to $74.41 a month, and 30% of households are energy challenged, stressed or impoverished. Xcel received 18 large load requests in 2024 against a usual two to three, and a state regulators' estimate projects residential rates could rise 55% by 2029 from 2024.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Democrats. Phil Weiser calls data centres a top priority for his first days in office.

Republicans. Victor Marx promises to "unleash our energy resources" to cut gas and utility bills.

Independents. Greg Lopez calls for "reliable, affordable energy" and a review of rising insurance costs.

Regulators. Xcel's proposed large load tariff would make data centres pay for their own power and grid upgrades; consumer advocates urge regulators to "check Xcel's math."

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: Energy costs give Marx a pocketbook attack, but Weiser is the heavy favourite. He beat Senator Michael Bennet in the primary with 56.9%. Unaffiliated voters, at over 2 million, outnumber either party.

Immigration.title: Colorado: Immigration (Fed)
Immigration.subtitle: ICE enforcement, the courts and state limits

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: Federal immigration enforcement in the Denver area has collided with Colorado courts and lawmakers. The issue is sharpest in the 8th District, one of the most closely fought House seats in the country.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: In May 2026 Judge R. Brooke Jackson found ICE violated his order limiting warrantless arrests and ordered officers retrained. The Denver ICE office makes about 15 to 25 arrests a day, and the Aurora detention centre holds an estimated 1,100 to 1,300 people. Lawmakers passed SB 5 to let people sue federal agents in state court, but Governor Jared Polis vetoed it, citing legal risks.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Republicans. Evans urges deporting "gangbangers, not grandmas" and questions ICE's use of administrative warrants. Governor nominee Victor Marx would end sanctuary policies and says, "Colorado will work with them, not against them."

Democrats. Manny Rutinel calls for an immediate overhaul of ICE and a pathway to citizenship. Hickenlooper vows to "go after ICE's violence."

Voters. About 4 in 10 voters in the 8th District are Hispanic, and Evans won it in 2024 by 2,449 votes.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: Immigration could decide the 8th District, which a Republican aligned poll showed nearly tied at 48% to 46%, with 51% disapproving of President Trump. Democrats see the seat as central to retaking the House.

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: Colorado Springs is losing U.S. Space Command headquarters to Huntsville, Alabama, after President Trump announced the move in September 2025. The state calls it political retaliation.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: Space Command expects about 200 people working in Huntsville by the end of 2026, up from about 20. A permanent headquarters could start construction in 2027 and finish in 2031. Colorado's lawsuit claims the move, along with cuts to energy funds and plans to dismantle the National Center for Atmospheric Research in Boulder, punishes the state for its mail voting system.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Democrats. Attorney General Phil Weiser, now the Democratic nominee for governor, brought the suit. His lawyers warn that accepting the administration's arguments "will change this country forever."

Republicans. Representative Jeff Crank says he is limiting the damage, noting that "Space Force jobs in the region have increased by more than 1,600 positions" in 18 months.

Local leaders. Colorado Springs and El Paso County officials formally opposed the lawsuit in January to focus on other bases.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: Weiser's lawsuit puts the move on the governor's ballot, against Republican Victor Marx, who runs a ministry in Colorado Springs. Senate challenger Mark Baisley, a former aerospace engineer for NASA and defence contractors, faces Senator John Hickenlooper, who won his primary with 52.8%.

Veterans.title: Colorado: Veterans (Fed)
Veterans.subtitle: VA staffing cuts and veterans' care

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: Colorado's large veteran population depends on a VA system that the Trump administration has shrunk. Staffing cuts, wait times and the shift toward private community care are now part of the state's federal races.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: About 334,000 veterans lived in Colorado in 2023. The VA first planned to cut about 82,000 workers, then scaled back to about 30,000, mostly through attrition. A federal workers' union counts a drop of over 44,000 VA employees in 2025.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Trump administration. VA Secretary Doug Collins defended the cuts at Aurora's regional hospital, saying, "The VA is the largest health care provider in this country. We're going to act like it."

Democrats. Senator John Hickenlooper called the cuts "egregious" and said, "You're not making government more efficient, you're making them less efficient."

Republicans. Representative Gabe Evans, an Army veteran, passed his first bill, BELO'S Act, giving National Park passes to families of veterans who died from service related causes.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: Veterans matter in the swing 8th District, where a poll for an Evans aligned group showed him ahead 48% to 46%. In the governor's race, Republican Marx, a Marine, and independent Greg Lopez, an Air Force veteran, both run on their service.

Detention.title: Florida: Detention (State)
Detention.subtitle: State run immigration detention and Alligator Alcatraz

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: Florida became the first state to run a facility only for immigration detainees when Alligator Alcatraz opened in the Everglades in July 2025. Its closure in June 2026 and unpaid costs have turned detention into a test of spending and accountability.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: Governor DeSantis said the site had zero detainees on 25 June. The state signed at least $1.01 billion in contracts, yet of $608 million in promised federal reimbursement it has received $58 million. Florida had first asked Washington for nearly $1.5 billion. A UNF poll found 57% of voters oppose new detention facilities.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Republicans. DeSantis says the site fulfilled its role and carried out about 21,000 deportations. He also opened a second site, the Deportation Depot, and Donalds runs as President Trump's endorsed ally.

Democrats. Jolly called the facility a callous political stunt, and Democratic lawmakers say its tents were never safe or humane.

Voters. Hispanic voters still narrowly favour Donalds 48% to 43%.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: Detention lets Democrats argue cost and competence rather than border policy alone. If federal reimbursement stays stalled, the remaining bill falls on the next governor's budget. For Republicans, the issue keeps enforcement, a strength with their base, in the headlines.

Drilling.title: Florida: Drilling (Fed)
Drilling.subtitle: Offshore drilling in the eastern Gulf

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: The Interior Department's draft 2026 to 2031 offshore leasing plan creates a new South Central Gulf area, opening the door to drilling off Florida for the first time in decades. Opposition in Florida is bipartisan, setting Florida Republicans against the Trump administration.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: The plan proposes two lease sales near Florida, in 2029 and 2030, at least 100 miles offshore. Federal waters in the eastern Gulf have been closed since 1995, and a first term Trump moratorium runs to 2032. Interior aimed to finalise the new programme by October 2026.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Republicans. Senators Rick Scott and Ashley Moody led the other 28 members of the delegation in opposing the plan, and Moody sponsors the American Shores Protection Act to codify the moratorium.

Democrats. Representative Debbie Wasserman Schultz called the plan horrendous, and Kathy Castor says it puts oil companies ahead of Florida's coast. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum insists there are no lease options near Florida.

Voters. Nearly 70% of Florida voters approved a constitutional ban on drilling in state waters.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: Drilling lets Florida Republicans show independence from President Trump. Moody, who leads Angie Nixon 50% to 40%, gains from leading the fight. A final plan that keeps Florida in before 3 November would hand Democrats a fresh argument.

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: Power bills have joined Florida's affordability debate after regulators approved the largest rate increase in the history of Florida Power & Light (FPL). The expected arrival of large data centres has turned utility regulation into campaign territory.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: The Public Service Commission approved a $7 billion increase over four years for about 6 million customer accounts. Typical bills in most of the state rise $2.50 a month in 2026 and reach $148.15 by 2029. The Office of Public Counsel, which represents customers, opposed the deal.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Democrats. Jolly calls for a statewide moratorium on new hyperscale data centres, citing environmental and public health concerns.

Republicans. Donalds proposes an AI bill of rights and echoes President Trump's view that presidential leadership keeps technology safe.

Voters. A Mason Dixon poll found 45% oppose data centres in Florida, against 38% in support.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: Power bills give Democrats a cost of living message that does not rely on national issues. FPL says new large load tariffs will keep data centre costs off household bills, while critics say those protections were watered down. The 2026 to 2029 rate plan spans most of the next governor's term.

Housing.title: Florida: Housing (State)
Housing.subtitle: Housing affordability and the condominium squeeze

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: Housing costs are Florida voters' top concern. Condo safety laws passed after the 2021 Surfside collapse forced older buildings to fund inspections, repairs and reserves, producing large special assessments that have pushed condo prices down.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: Housing costs topped a UNF list of voter concerns at 14%. Florida condo inventory has risen 35% since March 2024, with median prices down 4.5% to $315,000. A 2025 law allows a two year pause in reserve contributions after milestone inspections.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Republicans. DeSantis and the legislature eased the rules through HB 913, which passed unanimously, and Florida Realtors back Amendment 3 and its larger homestead exemption as relief.

Democrats. Jolly has made lowering housing and insurance costs central to his campaign.

Voters. 66% of Floridians worry they may not be able to afford their homes or communities because of property taxes or other housing costs.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: Condo distress is concentrated in older South Florida buildings, the only region where the Democratic Senate nominee leads. Housing also gives Jolly an opening with voters aged 18 to 34, who narrowly back him 48% to 46%. Republicans will cite the 2025 relief law and Amendment 3 as proof they are acting.

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: Property insurance is Florida's defining cost of living issue. After years of insurer exits and soaring premiums the market has stabilised, but bills remain high and the next governor will decide whether to keep or replace the current model.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: Citizens, the state insurer of last resort, will cut homeowners multiperil rates by an average 8.8% in 2026, and its policy count is down 76% from a 2023 peak of 1.41 million. A UNF poll found voters rank property insurance second only to housing costs.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Democrats. David Jolly would expand the state catastrophe fund using insurance profit taxes and tourist dollars so the state absorbs wind risk, targeting savings of 60 to 70%.

Republicans. Byron Donalds's Bring Down the Bill plan keeps the 2022 and 2023 reforms and continues shifting policies out of Citizens, promising savings of 20 to 25%. He brands Jolly's plan a $1,000 hurricane tax, citing a study of a different proposal.

Voters. Independents favour Jolly 47% to 28%.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: Insurance is the clearest policy contrast in a race where Donalds leads 48% to 41%. An ambitious state plan carries risk in a state that has not elected a Democratic governor since 1994, but it gives Jolly a concrete reason for voters to break with the status quo.

Lobbying.title: Florida: Lobbying (Fed)
Lobbying.subtitle: Foreign lobbying and the David Rivera case

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: Federal rules on foreign lobbying are in focus after former Republican Representative David Rivera was convicted under the Foreign Agents Registration Act (FARA). The case highlights Miami's role as a crossroads for foreign influence campaigns aimed at U.S. policy on Latin America.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: On 1 May, a Miami jury found Rivera and Esther Nuhfer guilty on all counts tied to a $50 million lobbying campaign for Venezuela's government. Prosecutors showed Rivera used about $600,000 of the proceeds for his congressional campaign. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, a longtime friend, testified he did not know Rivera was lobbying.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Republicans. The Trump administration's U.S. Attorney framed the case as a betrayal in a region where families fled communism, fitting Republican anti communist messaging.

Democrats. Jolly argues Florida has allowed corruption to run rampant and makes accountability a campaign theme.

Voters. Prosecutors said such betrayal carries real weight in South Florida, where many families fled communist rule.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: The verdict puts foreign money in Miami politics back in view as Republicans defend seats built on exile communities. With Hispanic voters still leaning to Moody 47% to 40%, there is no sign yet that it has shifted the bloc. Rivera's sentencing could revive the story near polling day.

Oversight.title: Florida: Oversight (State)
Oversight.subtitle: Florida DOGE audits and the property tax amendment

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: Florida's version of DOGE, rebranded the Florida Agency for Fiscal Oversight, audits city and county spending under Chief Financial Officer Blaise Ingoglia. It was built as a prelude to a property tax amendment now on the November ballot.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: Audits began in July 2025 with Broward County and Gainesville, two places that lean Democratic, and the state has threatened fines of $1,000 a day for each missing document. Amendment 3 would raise the homestead exemption to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028 and needs 60% to pass. A UNF poll found 61% support when voters heard it would limit local spending to core services.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Republicans. Ingoglia says local governments can absorb tax cuts and insists the audits are not going away.

Democrats. Democratic former Congressman Al Lawson and Republican Jeff Brandes call the ballot title politically loaded.

Local officials. County leaders say the audits lack context, including state mandated spending.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: Amendment 3 may lift turnout among older homeowners, and voters aged 65 and over already favour Donalds 51% to 35%. The 60% bar means it needs Democratic and independent votes to pass. The audits also give Republicans a spending message against Democratic run counties such as Broward.

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: Florida redrew its congressional map in 2026, between censuses, at Governor DeSantis's request after President Trump urged Republican states to strengthen the party's House majority. The new lines apply to this year's elections.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: The map could shift the delegation from 20 to 8 to 24 to 4 in favour of Republicans. It removes Democratic seats in Tampa, Orlando and two in the Fort Lauderdale area. Darren Soto's seat swings from a 58.8 Democratic lean to a 58.9 Republican lean.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Republicans. Lawmakers call the map legally sound, and a circuit judge suggested the old map may fail under a new Supreme Court ruling on race in redistricting.

Democrats. Equal Ground, Common Cause and the League of Women Voters say it breaches the Fair Districts Amendment ban on partisan maps. The Florida Supreme Court let the map stand in June.

Voters. Soto says the map targets Florida's 1.3 million Puerto Ricans, who are concentrated around Orlando.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: Four Democrats, Soto, Moskowitz, Wasserman Schultz and Castor, face redrawn seats. Jared Moskowitz's new 25th District is the least Republican of the targeted districts, making it Democrats' best chance to hold one. In a close national cycle, Florida's lines alone could swing House control.

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: Everglades restoration is a joint federal and state effort to send cleaner water south from Lake Okeechobee towards Florida Bay. Support is bipartisan, so the contest turns on who can sustain recent progress on its flagship project, the Everglades Agricultural Area (EAA) Reservoir.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: In April, officials confirmed all federally funded EAA Reservoir contracts were executed, moving completion to 2029, five years early, with more than $2 billion in federal funding. A House spending bill adds $446 million for restoration, and DeSantis cites nearly $8 billion in related funding since 2019.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Republicans. The Everglades Trust endorsed Donalds to maintain DeSantis's momentum, and he proposes a statewide water restoration grant programme modelled on the Everglades effort.

Democrats. Jolly ties restoration to an environmental economy built on pollution prevention and science.

Voters. The Everglades Trust estimates a four dollar return for every dollar invested in restoration.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: Because both sides back restoration, the issue rewards credibility rather than position. It matters most in communities hit by harmful Lake Okeechobee discharges, including Donalds's own Southwest Florida base. Faster federal delivery under the Trump administration lets Republicans claim results, while Democrats must argue they would protect the gains.

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: Gun policy is an early flashpoint in Florida's governor race. The 2018 Parkland school safety law raised the minimum age to buy long guns to 21, and a court ruling has since made open carry legal in practice.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: A three judge panel of the First District Court of Appeal struck down the open carry ban, yet the legislature did not write open carry into law in its 2026 session. The Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School Public Safety Commission ended its work this summer. Law enforcement opposition has so far blocked repeal of the age limit.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Republicans. Donalds says the age 21 rule has to go and celebrates the open carry ruling, calling Florida essentially an open carry state.

Democrats. Jolly says the Parkland law was bipartisan, backed by law enforcement and should stay, and promises new gun safety measures.

Voters. Pinellas County Sheriff Bob Gualtieri, who chaired the safety commission, supports Donalds.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: Guns sharpen a gender gap in which women back Jolly 49% to 41% and men favour Donalds by 22 points. Any repeal would still need the Florida Senate, which has acted as a bulwark on the 2018 law. The issue may help Jolly with suburban women while energising the Republican base.

Elections.title: Georgia: Elections (State)
Elections.subtitle: Election administration and the Fulton County fight

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: Control of Georgia's elections is contested again. A Republican majority State Election Board, an FBI seizure of Fulton County's 2020 ballots and calls for a state takeover of Fulton elections frame the 2026 vote.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: On 28 January, the FBI seized more than half a million 2020 ballots from Fulton's election hub. In May, a federal judge let the government keep them, although Georgia's 2020 vote was counted three times. Four of the board's five members are Republicans, and it has banned optical character recognition tallies, a technology Georgia's machines do not use.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Republicans. State Senator Greg Dolezal, nominee for lieutenant governor, says the state should take over Fulton elections, and Collins cheered the raid.

Democrats. Representative Saira Draper says controlling Fulton means controlling statewide outcomes. Ossoff defends voter ID while accusing Collins of undermining the 2020 result.

Voters. 11% of voters cite threats to democracy as their top issue.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: Fulton is Georgia's most populous county and heavily Democratic, so any change to how it runs elections could shape close statewide races. The lieutenant governor contest, where Democrat Josh McLaurin led Dolezal 48% to 44% in one poll, has become a proxy fight over that question.

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: Enhanced federal subsidies for Affordable Care Act (ACA) plans expired at the end of 2025. Georgia, which runs its own marketplace called Georgia Access, has seen one of the sharpest falls in coverage, putting health costs at the centre of the Senate race.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: Georgia Access enrolment fell from 1.5 million in January 2025 to 950,000 by April 2026, a 37% drop. In 2025, 93% of enrollees relied on the subsidies, and an estimated 460,000 Georgians could become uninsured by 2034.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Democrats. Ossoff fought to extend the subsidies and argues Collins's votes raised premiums. He also backs repealing recent Medicaid cuts.

Republicans. Collins points to more than $200 million he says he secured for rural hospitals and casts Ossoff as an elite, calling the contest Georgia against Georgetown.

Voters. Housing affordability and health care tie as the second most cited concern at 14%, behind only the economy.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: Health costs are Ossoff's strongest economic contrast and help explain his lead of 50% to 43% in one poll. Falling coverage also strains rural hospitals, carrying the issue beyond metro Atlanta into Republican leaning counties. Collins must defend the 2025 budget law, which also tightened marketplace rules.

Immigration.title: Georgia: Immigration (Fed)
Immigration.subtitle: Federal enforcement and the Hyundai plant raid

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: Federal immigration enforcement collided with Georgia's investment strategy in September 2025, when agents raided the Hyundai and LG battery plant site near Savannah. The issue divides Senator Jon Ossoff and Representative Mike Collins, author of the Laken Riley Act.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: Agents detained 475 workers, most of them South Korean, in what officials called the largest single site operation in Homeland Security history. Many were engineers and skilled workers, and construction has resumed. An Emerson poll found only 7% of voters rank immigration as their top issue.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Republicans. Collins backs President Trump's mass deportation campaign and says the southern border is now secure.

Democrats. Ossoff voted for the Laken Riley Act but criticises the raids, citing more than 1,000 cases of human rights abuse in detention documented by his office.

Voters. The economy leads voter concerns at 36%, far ahead of immigration.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html:
Immigration energises Collins's base, but economic issues dominate, which suits Ossoff, who leads 50% to 43% in one poll.

India and U.S. interests. The raid exposed gaps in visa routes for skilled foreign technicians on U.S. projects, a likely concern for Indian firms and professionals that rely on similar pathways.

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: Georgia is one of 10 states that have not fully expanded Medicaid. Its Pathways programme, which requires work or study, must change under the 2025 federal budget law, making coverage a defining issue in the governor's race.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: Pathways covers adults earning roughly $15,000 or less who log 80 hours a month; Georgia once said it would cover 300,000 people. Enrolment was 7,463 in May 2025, against a first year projection above 25,000. Federal work rules apply from January 2027, and Georgia wants an extra $1.4 billion from Washington, warning Pathways could otherwise end. The state projects enrolment could rise to nearly 120,000 under looser federal rules.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Democrats. Keisha Lance Bottoms calls Pathways broken and pledges full Medicaid expansion.

Republicans. Rick Jackson, a health care executive, rejects full expansion and would offer lawmakers a Pathways style programme with work requirements.

Voters. In states without expansion, more than half of rural hospitals operate in the red.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: Medicaid lets Bottoms carry a health message into rural Georgia, where she has campaigned outside a shuttered hospital. With Jackson ahead 48% to 45% in one September poll, small rural gains could decide the race.

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: Hurricane Helene hit South and East Central Georgia in September 2024, devastating farms and forests. Slow federal relief has made recovery a test of how well Washington serves rural Georgia.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: Helene caused an estimated $5.5 billion in agricultural damage, destroying about a third of pecan and cotton crops. Congress authorised block grants in December 2024, but growers waited nearly 18 months for Georgia's $531 million grant. The state saw 27 farm bankruptcies last year, more than double the year before.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Democrats. Ossoff notes Congress approved the aid before President Trump took office and pressed USDA after other states signed agreements first.

Republicans. Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins apologised for the delay and said the President stands with farmers, while state Agriculture Commissioner Tyler Harper rolled out the grants.

Voters. Farmers also face higher costs for fertiliser, equipment and fuel.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: Recovery gives Ossoff a rural economic argument, reinforced by his debate focus on foreign tariffs on farm exports such as pecans. Republicans counter that the money finally flowed under President Trump. The issue matters most in farm counties that usually vote Republican, where small swings can move a statewide result.

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: Year round sales of E15, petrol blended with 15% ethanol, would expand demand for Iowa corn. Iowa produces almost 30% of American ethanol, so the stalled federal bill is a direct farm economy issue in the open Senate race.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: The House passed the Nationwide Consumer and Fuel Retailer Choice Act in May, with all four Iowa members voting yes. The Senate version rode on a farm bill that the Senate Agriculture Committee failed to advance on 6 August over a SNAP dispute. Industry estimates say E15 could save drivers up to 30 cents a gallon.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Republicans. Ashley Hinson helped secure House passage and urged the Senate to send the bill to President Trump, who has said he would sign it.

Democrats. Josh Turek backs year round E15 and warns of a second farm crisis.

Opponents. Resistance comes mainly from senators of states with large oil and gas industries.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: Because both candidates back E15, the issue is about delivery. Hinson can claim House passage, while Turek can blame the Senate for stalling. Polls are split, with Fox News showing Turek ahead 49% to 47% and Suffolk showing Hinson ahead 45% to 41%, so farm income worries could move rural votes.

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: Federal Medicaid cuts in the 2025 budget law and the end of enhanced Affordable Care Act subsidies have put rural health care at the centre of Iowa's open Senate race.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: The law's Medicaid cuts total $1 trillion over a decade and take effect in 2027. Iowa facilities will receive $209 million from the Rural Health Transformation Program, meant to offset reduced rural Medicaid spending. A Reuters and Ipsos poll found health care was the cost voters most wanted Congress to address.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Democrats. Turek says Hinson voted for the largest Medicaid cut ever, claims 110,000 Iowans would lose coverage and attacks her vote against extending ACA subsidies.

Republicans. Hinson calls Medicaid rife with waste and abuse and points to the rural health funds and her work on pharmacy benefit managers.

Voters. In a Suffolk poll, health costs ranked third among household budget pressures at 22%.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: Turek leads among voters falling behind financially by 38 points, the group most exposed to health costs. Democrats also hope health care helps them win at least two Iowa House seats. With the Senate race within the margin of error, rural clinic closures could prove decisive.

Pipeline.title: Iowa: Pipeline (State)
Pipeline.subtitle: The Summit carbon pipeline and eminent domain

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: Summit Carbon Solutions plans a pipeline to capture carbon dioxide from ethanol plants and store it underground in North Dakota. Whether a private company may use eminent domain to cross Iowa farmland has split Republicans and made property rights a state campaign issue.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: The project would run about 2,500 miles across five states at an estimated $8.9 billion. In 2026 Summit dropped routes in eight Iowa counties, removing more than 400 landowners and about 200 miles, and it still works with 27 Iowa ethanol plants. Regulators now require approvals for a full route to the storage site before construction.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Republicans. The party is split. Governor Kim Reynolds vetoed a 2025 bill tightening pipeline rules, while several Republican primary candidates for governor pledged to ban eminent domain for carbon pipelines.

Industry. Ethanol groups call the project essential to Iowa agriculture and jobs.

Voters. The Iowa Farm Bureau asked regulators to restrict Summit's use of eminent domain until the project's viability is clear.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: Pipeline politics shadowed the Republican primary, which Zach Lahn won by fewer than 2,000 votes over Trump endorsed Randy Feenstra, a candidate unpopular with property rights activists. Rural anger over land seizures could still shape turnout in a governor's race where Rob Sand leads Lahn 53% to 44%.

Runoff.title: Iowa: Runoff (State)
Runoff.subtitle: Farm runoff and the voluntary nutrient strategy

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: Iowa relies on a voluntary Nutrient Reduction Strategy to cut nitrogen and phosphorus running off farmland. Critics say voluntary measures have failed, putting the state's light touch approach to agriculture under scrutiny.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: A two year assessment attributed 80% of nitrogen in central Iowa's watersheds to agriculture. The strategy is more than a decade old, and a 2023 review found no significant change in nitrogen levels. Nitrate levels in Iowa waters rank among the highest nationwide. The governor's package includes $52 million for cover crops, reduced tillage and wetlands, all voluntary.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Republicans. Senate committee leaders appear ready to keep the voluntary strategy, and farm groups say nitrate levels naturally fluctuate and remain relatively stable.

Democrats. House Minority Leader Brian Meyer pledged to finally deliver results on water quality, and environmental critics call the governor's package too little too late.

Voters. Even some farmers say voluntary conservation is not enough.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: Both nominees for governor favour incentives over mandates, so regulation itself is not on the ballot. The real test comes in the 2027 legislature, whose makeup this election decides. Lahn's backing from a Make America Healthy Again super PAC could nudge Republicans towards tougher action on farm pollution.

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: Nitrate pollution, mostly from farm fertiliser, threatens drinking water in central Iowa. Spikes have forced lawn watering bans around Des Moines, and rising cancer rates have made water quality a central issue in the governor's race.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: Iowa recorded 36 nitrate related drinking water violations in 2025, more than double 2024, against a federal limit of 10 milligrams per litre. Central Iowa Water Works, serving more than 600,000 people, ran its removal facility for more than 100 days in 2026. Iowa has the second highest cancer rate in the country.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Democrats. Rob Sand says nitrates can cause cancer and proposes tax incentives to turn farmland into wetlands, which filter water.

Republicans. Zach Lahn has made water and cancer central to his campaign, and both nominees back funding a water quality programme voters approved 16 years ago. Governor Reynolds announced a $100 million treatment package in May.

Voters. A poll led by Food & Water Action found 79% support mandatory pollution rules for industrial agriculture.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: Water is unusual because both nominees campaign on it, blurring the usual farm versus environment divide. The Des Moines and Raccoon rivers supply nearly 20% of Iowans, so the issue reaches the state's largest suburban vote. Sand leads Lahn 53% to 44% in the Fox News poll.

Detention.title: Illinois: Detention (Fed)
Detention.subtitle: Broadview and the fight over detention sites

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: Illinois has one ICE detention site, a processing centre in suburban Broadview. During Operation Midway Blitz it held people for days in conditions a federal judge condemned, and the state has since moved to block new facilities.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: Broadview was designed for 12 hour stays, but ICE allowed up to 72 hours from June 2025, and some detainees stayed for weeks. In November 2025 Judge Robert Gettleman ordered bedding, cleaning, meals and legal access, saying "It's really become a prison." Nationally, ICE has earmarked $38.3 billion to buy warehouses for detention, and DHS toured a 212,000 square foot warehouse a block from Broadview.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Democrats. Illinois enacted HB 5024, barring new detention centres within 1,500 feet of schools, homes, parks and places of worship. Sponsor Kimberly Lightford says families must be safe "from federal interference."

Republicans. Representative Patrick Windhorst argued the law "would be found unconstitutional" because state law cannot override federal authority. A law professor calls the question "up in the air."

Local government. Broadview says the blitz cost the village $361,536 and has asked Washington to reimburse it.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: Detention keeps enforcement visible in Chicago's western suburbs. Stratton backs abolishing ICE, while Tracy emphasises costs, healthcare and taxes. Pritzker, seeking a third term, leads Bailey by 20 points.

Immigration.title: Illinois: Immigration (Fed)
Immigration.subtitle: Operation Midway Blitz and its aftermath

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: The Chicago region became a national flashpoint when federal agents launched Operation Midway Blitz in September 2025. Its record now runs through Illinois' Senate and governor races.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: Over 68 days from 8 September to 14 November 2025, agents detained 3,841 people, and 2,732 of them have since been deported or left on their own. Only 15% had a prior conviction, down from about 50% just after the inauguration, and roughly 8 in 10 held had no criminal conviction.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Democrats. Senate nominee Juliana Stratton said "I want to abolish ICE," the only major primary candidate to do so. Governor JB Pritzker says some children remain "truly traumatized" and local economies have not fully recovered.

Republicans. Senate nominee Don Tracy says he is "not going to be a rubber stamp for anybody" and links Stratton to Bernie Sanders and Zohran Mamdani. Governor nominee Darren Bailey argues people "don't feel safe yet."

Trump administration. DHS says targets are chosen by legal status alone and calls the arrest data "cherry picked."

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: A Public Policy Polling survey put Pritzker ahead 54% to 34% over Bailey, a rematch of his 2022 win by 55% to 42%. In the open seat left by Dick Durbin, Tracy is casting Stratton's ICE stance as out of step.

Fishing.title: Maine: Fishing (Fed)
Fishing.subtitle: Lobster, trade and right whale rules

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: Lobster is Maine's most valuable fishery, and its future rests on federal decisions on trade and on right whale protection. Both have become tests of Senator Susan Collins's influence in Washington.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: Harvesters landed 78.8 million pounds worth $619 million in 2025, about seven million pounds less than 2024. In August, Canada dropped seafood from its retaliatory tariff list; nearly half of Maine's lobster goes to Canada for processing in the autumn. In September, the House passed a seven year extension of the pause on new gear rules.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Republicans. Collins says she urged U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer to return to talks with Canada, stressing that Canada is not China.

Democrats. Senate nominee Troy Jackson blamed Collins for failing to stop the renewed trade war.

Voters. Conservation groups warn only about 75 reproductive female right whales remain and hope the extension dies in the Senate.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: Any trade or gear shock would land on coastal communities just before polling day. Jackson leads Collins 51% to 47% in one poll, though 57% of voters still expect Collins to win. Trade has become Jackson's main line of attack on her record of delivering for the coast.

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: Maine's rural hospitals face staff shortages, falling births and federal Medicaid cuts. Maternity unit closures have become the most visible sign of strain and a shared concern for all three candidates for governor.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: Closing the birthing unit at Lincoln Hospital in Damariscotta would be the 12th maternity unit closure in Maine in a decade. Lincoln's births have fallen to about 130 a year from 200 two decades ago. Maine receives $190 million in Rural Health Transformation funds, which do not fully cover federal Medicaid cuts.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Republicans. Bobby Charles blames Pingree for MaineCare fraud and cost overruns and targets hundreds of millions in waste at the health department.

Democrats. Governor Mills asked MaineHealth to delay the Lincoln decision for two years, and all three candidates urged the hospital to keep the unit open.

Independents. Rick Bennett backs continued Medicaid expansion and says the state is shortchanging hospitals with delayed payments.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: Health care lets Charles and Bennett attack eight years of Democratic control, while Democrats tie hospital strain to federal cuts. With 44% of Mainers saying their finances worsened over the past year, care costs and access feed a wider affordability argument that each campaign is trying to own.

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: Maine faces a deep housing shortage driven by in migration, slow construction and rising prices. It is a central issue in the open governor's race, where all three candidates promise faster permitting.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: Maine is short about 84,000 homes. The median home costs $427,000, requiring an income of $102,000, against a median household income of $74,000. A 20% down payment on an average home is $80,000 or more.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Democrats. Pingree pledges $100 million a year for new and preserved homes, a 90 day deadline on state permits and limits on sales to out of state investors.

Republicans. Charles would cut regulations he calls over permitting and overreaching, lower income and property taxes, and cut energy costs by 40%.

Independents. Bennett offers down payment help for first time buyers, a revival of manufactured housing and deadlines for answering permit applications.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: Housing reaches younger voters and workers priced out of coastal towns. Pingree leads 52% to 40%, and 44% of Mainers say their finances worsened in the past year, so cost of living messages carry weight. Charles is betting that deregulation and tax cuts can win over voters frustrated with eight years of Democratic rule.

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: Maine leads the country in confronting PFAS, the forever chemicals spread on farmland for decades through sludge fertiliser. Responsibility is shared, with the state funding farm support while Congress and the EPA set national rules.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: Maine banned sludge spreading in 2022, and its agriculture department is working with 127 sites, recently adding $3 million in research grants. Maine has more than 30,000 PFAS records at close to 250 sites. In May, the EPA proposed to rescind four PFAS limits and delay PFOA and PFOS compliance to 2031.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Republicans. Collins reintroduced the Relief for Farmers Hit with PFAS Act with Democratic Representative Chellie Pingree to fund state aid, testing and farm relocation.

Democrats. Senator Angus King and Representative Jared Golden are original cosponsors, making PFAS a rare bipartisan Maine cause.

Voters. Farm advocates say nearly all of the first 59 affected farms made a safe transition with state support.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: PFAS gives Collins a bipartisan record to cite, while Democrats can tie the EPA rollback to the Trump administration. If federal limits weaken, Maine's own fund and rules become the main protection for affected farmers, raising the stakes of the governor's race.

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: The 1980 Maine Indian Claims Settlement Act treats the four Wabanaki Nations more like municipalities than sovereign nations. Restoring their sovereignty has become a clear dividing line between Governor Mills and those seeking to succeed her.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: In 2025 the legislature passed LD 958, barring the state from taking tribal land by eminent domain, 86 to 60 in the House and 20 to 12 in the Senate. Mills vetoed it, preferring piecemeal changes. The country's 570 other federally recognised tribes are not bound by a similar arrangement.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Democrats. Hannah Pingree supports fully restoring sovereignty, calls it her main difference with Mills and promises action in her first 100 days. Troy Jackson, now the Senate nominee, pledged a restoration bill on day one as a candidate for governor.

Republicans. Bobby Charles would not say whether he backs restoration, noting Maine's system differs from the rest of the country.

Independents. Rick Bennett also supports full restoration.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: Pingree expects endorsements from four tribal chiefs, marking a generational shift inside the Democratic Party. A Pingree win would likely bring a sovereignty bill in 2027, while a Charles win would stall it. Bennett's support means two of the three candidates back full restoration.

Wind.title: Maine: Wind (Fed)
Wind.subtitle: Offshore wind in the Gulf of Maine

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: Maine once aimed to lead the country in floating offshore wind in the Gulf of Maine. The Trump administration has halted federal research money and bought back leases, turning the industry into a federal policy fight.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: In April 2025, the Energy Department halted $15.8 million in University of Maine wind research, weeks before a floating turbine launch off Castine. In 2026, Interior ended two Gulf of Maine leases through a buyback deal with Invenergy. Maine's attorney general co led eight states in a notice of intent to sue.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Republicans. Republican state lawmakers asked the administration to revoke Gulf of Maine leases. Collins's office said the administration simply has different energy priorities. Bobby Charles, the nominee for governor, would expand natural gas and end solar subsidies.

Democrats. Governor Janet Mills called the buyback an egregious waste of taxpayer money and legally questionable.

Voters. Independent Rick Bennett wants to cut dependence on fossil fuels through regional renewables.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: Wind divides the coast, since many fishermen opposed the federal lease sales even as the state planned a turbine port. With Democrat Hannah Pingree leading Charles 52% to 40%, Maine is likely to keep backing renewables, but without federal partners.

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: Michigan's auto industry sits at the centre of President Trump's tariff policy. Federal tariffs on Canada and on foreign cars cut both ways for a state built on cross border supply chains, while state leaders compete over who can protect auto jobs.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: Michigan lost nearly 4,000 auto parts jobs in the year to June 2026, while vehicle assembly added about 500. GM projects $2.5 to $3.5 billion in tariff costs this year. The administration placed 50% tariffs on $27.6 billion in Canadian goods.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Republicans. President Trump credits tariffs for rising GM output. Senate nominee Mike Rogers backed them but now says Canada is not our enemy and wants the tariff war ended.

Democrats. Abdul El-Sayed says Rogers cheered the trade war and is now reversing course. Benson proposes a Michigan deal with Canada that experts doubt is legally possible.

Voters. The UAW backs targeted tariffs but says Canada is not the problem.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: A taxpayer group estimates tariffs cost Michigan households $5,600 a year, the third highest in the nation. With El-Sayed ahead 50% to 45% and Rogers distancing himself from the President, tariffs are the clearest sign of Republican vulnerability in Michigan.

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: Great Lakes shipping depends on Coast Guard icebreakers to move iron ore and other cargo in winter. An ageing and undersized fleet has left Michigan lawmakers pressing for a new heavy icebreaker.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: U.S. flagged ships lost 82 ship days, about a third of the 2026 season, to inadequate icebreaking. The Mackinaw is the only heavy icebreaker on the Lakes, and the fleet has 11 vessels, down from 20 nearly 50 years ago. A new heavy icebreaker could cost up to $350 million; about $80 million has been appropriated for early work.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Democrats. Representative Kristen McDonald Rivet led a delegation letter urging the Coast Guard to start work, and Senator Gary Peters secured $25 million in Coast Guard funds.

Republicans. Heavy icebreaker money was in early drafts of the 2025 budget law but was cut from the final version.

Industry. The Lake Carriers Association says the region has received nickels and dimes when it needs far larger sums.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: Icebreaking ties Michigan's industrial economy to federal budgets, since nearly all U.S. domestic iron ore passes through the Soo Locks. It is a bipartisan local cause, so the political test is whether the next Congress funds a ship that Michigan has sought for years.

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: Selfridge Air National Guard Base in Macomb County was losing its A-10 mission and faced an uncertain future until President Trump announced a new fighter mission in April 2025. The base is a bipartisan priority and a symbol of federal investment in Michigan.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: Selfridge will receive 21 F-15EX fighters, with the first due in 2028 and KC-46 tankers from 2030. The base faces about $985 million in new construction through 2031. Senator Gary Peters says it supports about 5,000 jobs and $850 million for the state economy.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Republicans. President Trump promised to save the base and make it better, and thanked Governor Whitmer for raising it with him.
