Democrats. Whitmer joined the President at Selfridge and thanked him for the recapitalisation, a rare bipartisan moment.

Voters. Many of the base's airmen recently returned from or remain on deployment in the U.S. Central Command region.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: Selfridge gives Republicans a concrete delivery story in Macomb County, where President Trump held a rally the same day as his announcement. Because Whitmer shares the credit, its partisan edge is limited, but it helps Republicans argue that federal ties bring jobs home.

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: The Palisades plant on Lake Michigan is set to become the first shuttered U.S. reactor to restart, backed by federal money. Its delays and plans for new small reactors make it a test of federal nuclear policy in Michigan.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: Holtec secured a federal loan of over $1.5 billion, and the plant could power more than 800,000 homes. An early 2026 reconnection target passed, and Holtec's chief executive expects a restart ahead of a March 2027 supply contract. Fuel loading began on 30 August but was paused after an incident, and regulators later found a chilled work environment.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Republicans. James includes nuclear in an energy strategy using every source and wants to repeal the state's clean energy mandate.

Democrats. Benson supports the 2023 clean energy law, saying it can put Michigan in a position to lead the nation.

Voters. Environmental groups that challenged the restart lost when a federal court dismissed their suit.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: Both parties back Palisades, so its fate is about competence, not direction. A safe restart before November would let the Trump administration and Michigan Democrats share credit, while further setbacks could feed doubts about Holtec's plan for two small reactors producing power by 2031.

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: Michigan adopted some of the nation's first state drinking water limits for PFAS in 2020. Adopted under Governor Gretchen Whitmer, they have been left legally fragile by a long court fight with 3M, making PFAS protection a state responsibility in flux.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: Michigan has 280 known or suspected PFAS sites. Appeals judges have twice ruled that regulators skipped a required cost analysis, most recently in September 2025, though the standards stayed in force during appeals. The EPA has proposed to delay key federal PFAS deadlines to 2031.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Democrats. Attorney General Nessel has defended the science based standards and is suing 3M separately; Benson pledges to hold polluters accountable.

Republicans. James has not set out a PFAS plan; his wider pitch is to stop using energy providers as political targets.

Industry. 3M called the rulemaking rushed and invalid.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: The next governor and attorney general will decide whether to rewrite the rules with a cost analysis or keep fighting in court. If federal limits weaken, Michigan's standards become the main protection for its residents, raising the stakes of down ballot races as well as the top of the ticket.

Pipeline.title: Michigan: Pipeline (State)
Pipeline.subtitle: Line 5 under the Straits of Mackinac

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: Enbridge's Line 5 carries oil and natural gas liquids through twin pipelines under the Straits of Mackinac. Democrats want it shut, Enbridge wants a tunnel to enclose it, and the next governor and attorney general will shape the outcome.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: Built in 1953, Line 5 moves up to 540,000 barrels a day across a 4.5 mile Straits crossing. In August, the Army Corps approved the tunnel permit, but the state Supreme Court found regulators erred in approving it. The tunnel was estimated at $500 million in 2018; one think tank expects at least three times that.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Democrats. Attorney General Dana Nessel's lawsuit seeks to shut Line 5, and Jocelyn Benson lists it among threats to the Great Lakes.

Republicans. John James would end state litigation against the tunnel and stop using energy providers as political targets.

Voters. The Army Corps acknowledged major, permanent harm to a Straits cultural landscape sacred to Anishinaabe peoples.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: Line 5 pits energy supply against Great Lakes protection, and Canada says Michigan is violating a treaty on the pipeline. With Benson ahead of James 52% to 43% in one poll, a Democratic win would keep the state's legal fight alive, while a James win would likely end it.

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: Electricity costs and a wave of AI data centres have made utility regulation a major Michigan issue. Households face repeated rate requests as utilities court very large new customers.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: Regulators approved a $242 million DTE increase in February, and DTE soon sought $474.3 million more, a 9.7% residential rise. Oracle's 1.4 gigawatt data centre in Saline Township won conditional approval for DTE power contracts. Attorney General Nessel called DTE's offer to pause rate requests a ransom note. Michigan's average home electric bill of $119.31 in 2024 was still below the national average.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Democrats. Benson backs a statewide data centre moratorium while protections are drawn up and supports the 2023 clean energy law.

Republicans. James would let communities decide on data centres, replace Public Service Commission members he says rubber stamp rate rises, and repeal the clean energy mandate.

Independents. Mike Duggan says a data centre may come only if it pays 100% of its utility costs.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: Power bills give every candidate an affordability message. Benson faces scrutiny over her husband's past work linked to the Saline project, while James has shifted on whether to back a moratorium. Voters in townships facing new projects may judge candidates on this issue alone.

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: Montana's housing costs soared as newcomers arrived after 2020. The state's response, the Montana Miracle zoning reforms, now faces its first real test as prices stay out of reach for many residents.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: The median home price peaked at $523,900 in summer 2023, with the income needed to buy reaching $141,000. In March 2026, the state Supreme Court unanimously upheld the 2023 zoning reforms allowing duplexes and accessory dwelling units. Advocates estimate a shortfall of about 15,000 rental units for low income households.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Republicans. Governor Greg Gianforte called the ruling a landmark victory, and House nominee Aaron Flint blames costs on inflation, saying big government created this crisis.

Democrats. Sam Forstag calls housing his top priority and would ban corporate ownership of homes and stop private equity buying mobile home parks.

Voters. Some homeowners sued to block the reforms, fearing new density in their neighbourhoods.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: Zoning reform passed with near unanimous support, so the partisan fight is over causes and corporate buyers rather than density. Housing is Forstag's lead argument in the competitive western district, where Flint also backs a Trump plan to bar Wall Street firms from buying family homes.

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: Federal public lands are central to Montana's economy. Proposals to sell federal land and loosen protections have made public lands a defining issue in the open Senate race and the western House race.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: In 2025, Senator Mike Lee's plan to sell up to 1.2 million acres of federal land was stripped from the budget law after opposition from Montana's delegation. In August 2026, the administration moved to repeal the Roadless Rule, which covers more than 6.4 million Montana acres. Senator Steve Daines withdrew from his reelection race in March.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Republicans. Senate nominee Kurt Alme vows to keep public lands in public hands. House nominee Aaron Flint says the same today but backed transferring federal land to the state in 2014 and 2015.

Democrats. Senate nominee Alani Bankhead says Republicans are opening public lands to AI data centres, and House nominee Sam Forstag also pledges protection.

Independents. Seth Bodnar promises to fight hard to defend public lands, and the state Democratic chair stepped down to endorse an independent for the Senate.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: Because every major candidate now claims to defend public lands, the contest is about credibility. Flint's past comments give Democrats an opening in a western district rated lean Republican by two forecasters but moved to toss up by Fox News.

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: Property taxes spiked in 2023 and led Montana to overhaul its system in 2025, shifting the burden from primary homes towards second homes and businesses. Whether that shift was fair will shape the 2027 legislative session.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: The 2025 reform lowered bills for 80% of residents. Primary homes valued at up to $400,000 are taxed at 1.4%, and higher values at 1.89%, while some businesses reported increases of about 30%. A Republican plan to cap annual increases at 2% was suspended in June.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Republicans. Senator Wylie Galt, who sponsored the reform, dropped his cap initiative to seek a broader fix in 2027 and warned he may be back if relief falls short.

Democrats. Democrats blamed the 2023 spike on the governor and Republican legislature and pushed a homestead exemption and a tax credit for renters and retirees.

Voters. Owners of high value homes and many small businesses saw large increases.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: Property taxes are a state legislative issue, so November's legislative races decide the 2027 approach. Business owners facing higher bills, such as a Kalispell brewery paying nearly $1,000 more a month, give Democrats and some Republicans a reason to revisit the 2025 shift.

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: Grizzly bears in the lower 48 states remain protected as threatened under federal law. Montana, Wyoming and Idaho want them removed from the list and handed to state management, making wildlife a federal and state flashpoint.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: A federal judge moved the delisting decision deadline to 28 December 2026. Grizzlies remain listed as threatened until the Fish and Wildlife Service makes its final decision. Federal estimates put both the Northern Continental Divide and Greater Yellowstone populations at more than 1,000 bears each.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Republicans. State officials say bear numbers have recovered and want management moved to the states.

Democrats and advocates. Wildlife groups say bears occupy only a small fraction of their historic range and fear hunting could slow recovery.

Independents. Seth Bodnar ties wildlife to protecting key habitat areas and species on public lands.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: Grizzlies matter most in rural western Montana, home to the state's most competitive House race. Because the federal decision falls after polling day, the next Congress and the state's leaders will manage the fallout, including any court challenge. A delisting could open the door to state managed hunts, which advocates fear would slow the species' recovery.

Healthcare.title: North Carolina: Healthcare (Fed)
Healthcare.subtitle: Affordable Care Act coverage and costs

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: The end of enhanced federal subsidies for Affordable Care Act plans and federal Medicaid cuts have raised health costs across North Carolina, making health care a central contrast in the Senate race.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: Marketplace sign ups fell from 975,110 in 2025 to 761,457 in 2026, a 22% drop and one of the largest in the country, as navigators reported many people could not afford a plan. About 9% of 2025 enrollees nationwide are now uninsured. Rural hospitals are projected to lose $3.7 billion under the 2025 budget law.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Democrats. Cooper strongly opposes Medicaid cuts that shift costs onto families and stresses rural dependence on care.

Republicans. Whatley has endorsed congressional Republican proposals to cut health subsidies and backed the President's tax agenda.

Voters. Economy and health care rank as very important to 73% of voters.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: Health care lets Cooper extend his affordability message to rural counties, where hospitals depend heavily on Medicaid payments. Senator Thom Tillis voted against the 2025 law partly over its risk to expansion enrollees, giving Cooper a Republican ally on the issue. Whatley must defend cuts while running far behind in the polls.

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: North Carolina's factories rely on both federal trade policy and state incentives. Tariffs meant to revive furniture and textile jobs have collided with rising costs, making manufacturing a test of President Trump's trade agenda.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: Manufacturing was the only major industry to shrink in the year to July 2025, losing nearly 9,000 jobs. Furniture tariffs of 25% took effect in October 2025, yet one firm with nine factories could not fill 50 jobs. In February the Supreme Court ruled emergency tariffs unlawful.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Democrats. Cooper pledges to vote to roll back the tariffs, saying trade authority rests with Congress.

Republicans. Whatley has said he supports the tariffs wholeheartedly and that they will create jobs and raise wages.

Voters. A John Locke Foundation report estimated tariffs cost the state's farms $695 million and 8,000 jobs.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: Manufacturing towns across the state feel both the tariff costs and the promised protection. Even North Carolina Republicans are split, with 77% saying tariffs help the economy but only 40% saying they help them personally. That gap gives Cooper room to argue costs over promises, while Whatley bets voters will credit tariffs for future factory investment.

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: North Carolina expanded Medicaid in 2023 with bipartisan support, but funding fights between Governor Stein and the Republican legislature and new federal rules have put the programme under strain.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: About 713,755 people are covered through expansion. In April, Stein signed a $319 million funding bill that also sets work rules of 80 hours a month for expansion adults. Health officials warn a provision could remove 27,000 children and pregnant women. State law ends expansion if the federal government stops paying 90% of its cost.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Democrats. Stein said the bill fully funds Medicaid but urged lawmakers to revisit its three month lookback rule.

Republicans. Senator Benton Sawrey said the bill gives Medicaid partners important tools and promised to fix any coverage gap.

Voters. Fourteen patient groups warned the lookback poses undue paperwork barriers.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: Medicaid ties state legislative races to the federal debate, since the General Assembly decides how far to cushion federal changes. The trigger law means a future federal cut could end expansion automatically. Rural hospitals, which stand to lose $3.7 billion under the federal law, make the issue potent in Republican leaning counties.

PFAS.title: North Carolina: PFAS (Mixed)
PFAS.subtitle: GenX and the Cape Fear River

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: Chemours and DuPont released GenX and other PFAS into the Cape Fear River for decades from a plant near Fayetteville. Cleanup depends on both state enforcement and federal action, which now diverge.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: The Cape Fear River supplies drinking water to at least 500,000 people downstream. A proposed EPA settlement would have Chemours pay up to $90 million over 15 years across three states, with no money required for North Carolina. A 2019 state consent order already requires Chemours to cut emissions and filter contaminated wells.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Democrats. Stein says the deal does nothing meaningful for North Carolinians, and Attorney General Jeff Jackson called it an insult to eastern North Carolina.

Republicans. The Trump administration's EPA negotiated the settlement, and Stein says it has weakened protections against chemicals like GenX.

Voters. State officials have gone to court to oppose the deal.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: PFAS matters most in the Wilmington and Fayetteville areas along the river. It lets Democrats contrast state enforcement with a federal retreat, and puts Republicans in the awkward position of defending an EPA deal that sends little money to the state. The environment ranks lower than the economy, at 43% calling it very important, but local salience is high.

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: Hurricane Helene devastated western North Carolina in 2024. Recovery depends on both federal aid from Congress and state spending, and the slow pace has become a central fight in the Senate race.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: Federal aid covers about 15% of an estimated $60 billion in damage. In June, Governor Josh Stein cut his request for more federal help from $13.48 billion to $10 billion, and more than 2,000 housing applicants will go unserved without new money. Congress has approved no new Helene aid since December 2024.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Democrats. Roy Cooper says Michael Whatley, a member of President Trump's FEMA Review Council, has not convinced the administration to include Helene money in its spending request.

Republicans. Whatley's campaign says he helped deliver $10.5 billion for western North Carolina and calls Cooper a failure on recovery.

Voters. Republican Senator Ted Budd vowed to oppose any spending bill without Helene funding.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: Recovery cuts across party lines in mountain counties that usually vote Republican. Cooper leads Whatley 49% to 38% in the Elon poll, and a stalled aid package lets him tie Whatley to the administration. Whatley needs visible federal progress before polling day.

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: North Carolina's Republican legislature redrew the state's congressional map in October 2025 to add one more Republican seat. The change targets Democrat Don Davis's eastern 1st District for 2026.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: The new lines move Dare, Hyde and other counties into the 1st District, shifting it from a Biden lean of 2 points to a Trump lean of 7. The delegation stands at 10 Republicans and 4 Democrats. A federal panel found plaintiffs had not clearly shown racial intent and let the map stand.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Republicans. Legislative leaders openly sought to add a Republican seat and remove a Democratic one.

Democrats. Civil rights groups argued the map is racially discriminatory, and Davis is running in the redrawn district.

Voters. An NRCC poll shows Davis and Republican Laurie Buckhout tied at 41%, with 17% undecided.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: The 1st District is one of the most consequential House races in the country. Because its lean is modest, Davis can still win with strong Democratic turnout in a good Democratic year. A statewide Cooper lead could help him, while a Buckhout win would deliver the seat the map was drawn to produce.

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: The August 2025 killing of Ukrainian refugee Iryna Zarutska on a Charlotte light rail train led to sweeping changes in pretrial release law. Public safety has since become Republicans' main line of attack in the Senate race.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: Iryna's Law passed the House 81 to 31 and the Senate 28 to 8, and Stein signed it in October 2025. It ends cashless release for many violent or repeat offenders, requires judges to weigh full criminal histories and limits death penalty appeals to two years. It took effect on 1 December 2025.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Republicans. Whatley says Cooper appointed magistrates and judges who keep a revolving door rolling and has won endorsements from troopers and police groups.

Democrats. Cooper's campaign says he spent his career jailing violent criminals and signed tougher bail laws as governor.

Voters. Mecklenburg Sheriff Gary McFadden warned of unintended costs such as overtime and prisoner transport.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: Crime is Whatley's best chance to shift a race where Cooper leads by 11 points. Because Stein, a Democrat, signed Iryna's Law, Republicans cannot easily cast Democrats as opposed to reform. Immigration, often linked to crime in Republican messaging, is very important to 54% of voters.

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: Nebraska's meatpacking towns depend on immigrant labour, yet the state has also become a partner in federal detention. Immigration enforcement is a dividing line in the Senate race between Pete Ricketts and independent Dan Osborn.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: A 2025 raid on Omaha's Glenn Valley Foods saw 75 to 80 people taken into custody, by Representative Don Bacon's count. Nebraska converted a McCook work camp into an ICE facility for up to 300 detainees, expected to earn the state about $14 million a year. ICE is now the nation's highest funded law enforcement agency.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Republicans. Ricketts says the border is secure and immigration laws are being enforced, and calls E-Verify not perfect.

Independents. Osborn backs strong border security and mandatory E-Verify but calls the ICE funding increase wasteful. In a leaked recording he called the border wall a symbol of racism.

Voters. Protesters still travel to McCook, while Pillen has doubled down on the facility.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: Osborn says the Big Four meatpackers benefit from a wide open border, casting immigration as a corporate issue. Ricketts hopes enforcement keeps Republicans united in a state where they outnumber Democrats roughly two to one. With Osborn ahead 46% to 42% in one poll, the issue could decide a close race.

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: Nebraska became the first state to enforce the federal Medicaid work requirements in the 2025 budget law, months ahead of the national deadline. Early coverage losses are now a test of the law in the Senate race.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: Enforcement began on 1 May 2026, about eight months before the January 2027 federal deadline, and more than 25,000 residents are expected to lose coverage. Early state data show at least 1,090 people lost coverage or were denied, with 92% of renewal losses due to missing paperwork.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Republicans. Ricketts voted for the 2025 budget law, calling it a once in a generation opportunity, and the state says its rollout protects eligible members.

Independents. Osborn opposes the law, saying Congress spends its time on tax cuts for billionaires.

Voters. The Nebraska Hospital Association warned the law creates uncertainty for hospitals on razor thin margins.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: Nebraska's early start means voters see coverage losses before polling day, unlike most states. Paperwork denials undercut the claim that only those unwilling to work lose coverage. Osborn's lead among working class voters, in a race he leads 46% to 42% in one poll, makes Medicaid a live issue.

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: Offutt Air Force Base near Omaha is home to U.S. Strategic Command and the 55th Wing. New nuclear command missions make it a major federal investment in the competitive 2nd District and a point of bipartisan pride.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: Offutt will host the new E-4C Survivable Airborne Operations Center, with $1.8 billion for aircraft development in a 2025 House spending bill. Earlier, $110 million funded planning for its hangars and facilities. The Air Force also chose Offutt for a new 95th Wing to centralise nuclear command and control.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Republicans. Ricketts welcomed the new wing, and retiring Representative Don Bacon said it would strengthen command of the nuclear deterrent.

Democrats. The base sits in the 2nd District, where Democrat Denise Powell faces Republican Brinker Harding for Bacon's open seat.

Voters. Senator Deb Fischer says Nebraska is proud of its leading role in national defence.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: Because Offutt enjoys support from both parties, the issue rewards incumbency and experience. Forecasters rate the 2nd District a lean or likely Democratic pickup, so Republicans may lean on defence spending to hold Omaha's suburbs. Bacon's retirement removes a veteran voice on Offutt from the delegation.

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: Nebraska's farm economy depends on exports, so federal trade policy shapes rural incomes. Tariff battles with China and a plan to import more foreign beef have put agriculture at the heart of the Senate race.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: In May, the administration said China agreed to buy at least $17 billion a year of U.S. farm goods through 2028, yet China bought $3.9 billion of non soybean farm products in the first seven months of 2026. The U.S. and China trade truce expires in November. The administration's plan to import more foreign beef has particularly roiled Nebraska agriculture.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Republicans. Ricketts defends wide tariffs as levelling the playing field but opposes the beef import plan and has pressed for more Chinese purchases.

Independents. Osborn criticises President Trump's trade wars and wants blanket tariffs replaced with strategic ones; he has used the beef plan in a new advertisement.

Voters. Political scientist Kevin Smith says Nebraska cattlemen were not happy about the beef imports.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: Trade lets Osborn reach Republican leaning farm voters without joining the Democratic Party. The China truce deadline falls in November, close to polling day, so any breakdown would land on Ricketts. A Trump visit to Grand Island in October showed Republican concern.

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: Property taxes are Nebraska's most persistent state issue, weighing on farmers and homeowners alike. Repeated attempts at relief have stalled in the legislature, and the problem now sits at the centre of the governor's race.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: Statewide property taxes have risen 241% since 2000, against income growth of about 106%, and rose 5.39% in the past year alone, a $286 million increase. The 2026 session ended without major new relief, with Governor Jim Pillen urging lawmakers to solve this decades old problem in 2027. A petition to put property tax changes on the November ballot ended in June.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Republicans. Pillen backs a firm annual cap on valuation and local spending increases, is open to a constitutional amendment and wants to repeal sales tax exemptions to fund relief.

Democrats. Lynne Walz proposes a universal homestead exemption on the first $100,000 of value and a valuation cap, targeting relief at residents rather than out of state investors.

Voters. The Farm Bureau backs a 2% cap, which it says would save about $1.5 billion by 2035.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: Property taxes are the main test of Pillen's record after four years in office. A poll for the Walz campaign put him ahead only 38% to 33%, with 58% saying the state is on the wrong track.

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: Nebraska faces two water problems at once. It is suing Colorado over the South Platte River and building a canal to claim its share, while nitrate pollution from farming threatens the groundwater most residents drink.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: In June 2026 the U.S. Supreme Court agreed to hear Nebraska's case against Colorado under the 1923 compact. Lawmakers set aside roughly $500 million for the Perkins County Canal, which is due online by the end of 2032. Groundwater supplies 85% of Nebraskans' drinking water.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Republicans. Attorney General Mike Hilgers calls the compact case the most important his office will handle for generations, and Pillen, a hog farmer, admitted farmers over applied fertiliser and water.

Democrats. State Senator Danielle Conrad called Pillen's new water agency a rebranding, and some lawmakers urged cuts to canal spending during the budget deficit.

Voters. A Colorado county commissioner warns the canal could dry irrigated land and raise eminent domain fears.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: Water ties rural health to the governor's record, since monitoring wells at some Pillen linked hog farms have shown nitrate well above the legal limit. The canal is popular as a defence of state rights, so Democrats focus on pollution and budget priorities instead. The Supreme Court case will outlast this election.

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: New Hampshire has some of the country's highest electricity prices, and the state has shifted its energy policy towards nuclear and natural gas. Power bills are a sharp contrast between Ayotte and Warmington.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: Eversource's default supply rate rose 23.94% on 1 August, from 11.3 to 14.0 cents per kilowatt hour. New Hampshire has the eighth highest residential electricity rates in the country. In 2025 the state refocused its energy strategy on nuclear and abolished its offshore wind office.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Republicans. Ayotte calls Gulf of Maine offshore wind too expensive and a risk to fishing, and supports expanding natural gas and nuclear options.

Democrats. Warmington blames high rates on Ayotte's addiction to fossil fuels and is updating a plan that aimed for net zero emissions by 2040.

Voters. A Republican energy committee chair blames limited gas access for high prices, while a Republican state senator says deregulation never produced competition.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: The August rate rise came just weeks before voting, giving Warmington a fresh cost of living argument. Ayotte answers that clean energy mandates would raise bills further. Eversource has deferred some costs that it will recover later, so bills may rise again during the next governor's term.

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: New Hampshire's housing market is among the tightest in New England, with record prices and very few homes for sale. Housing costs are a central theme in the race between Governor Kelly Ayotte and Democrat Cinde Warmington.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: The median single family home reached a record $565,000, up 68% since June 2020, and buyers need about $182,000 a year to afford it. Statewide listings fell from about 8,000 a decade ago to below 3,000. A 2025 law requires towns to allow multifamily housing in commercial zones.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Republicans. Ayotte proposes leasing surplus state land for homes and converting unused offices, saying she wants more creative ways to expand housing.

Democrats. Warmington attacks sky high prices and supports state efforts to remove local zoning barriers.

Voters. Only about 15% of households earn enough to afford the median home.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: Housing lets Warmington press an affordability case against an incumbent, while Ayotte can point to zoning reform and record permitting. Ayotte leads 47% to 43% in the Granite State Poll. Younger voters priced out of the market could tip a close race, and property taxes that have doubled for some owners add to the pressure.

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: New Hampshire was one of the first states to set its own PFAS drinking water limits after contamination around the former Saint Gobain plant in Merrimack. With federal rules now weakening, state action and costs carry more weight.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: The state limits are 12 parts per trillion for PFOA and 15 for PFOS, and a 2024 law bans added PFAS in many consumer goods from 2027. Londonderry estimates PFAS will cost it more than $275 million, against about $50 million in state aid. The EPA has delayed federal compliance deadlines.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Republicans. Attorney General John Formella calls a Saint Gobain payment toward a water main another step to hold the company accountable.

Democrats. Democratic Representative Karen Ebel sponsored the 2024 consumer ban, which passed with bipartisan support.

Voters. Londonderry's town manager says the response will continue to take more taxpayer dollars.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: PFAS is a bipartisan concern, so it rewards record rather than rhetoric. Rising local costs feed into property taxes, which already provide 61% of local revenue, the highest share of any state. A weaker federal rule shifts the burden to the next governor and legislature.

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: Education Freedom Accounts give families state money for private schooling and other education costs. Ayotte signed a law removing income limits in 2025, turning the programme into a near universal voucher and a defining line in the governor's race.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: Enrolment rose from 5,765 students to 10,510 after income limits ended, and only 343 of them had attended a public school the year before. Each student received about $4,911 in 2025 to 2026. The cap rises to 12,500 next year, and Democrats warn the cost could reach over $100 million a year.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Republicans. Ayotte signed the expansion and a later law opening public school courses to account holders, while some Republicans now seek tighter audits.

Democrats. Warmington opposes diverting public education funds, saying it raises property taxes.

Voters. About two dozen towns have passed resolutions urging limits based on financial need.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: Vouchers link education to property taxes, a sensitive issue in a state that funds schools mainly through local levies. Most new recipients were already outside public schools, which strengthens Democrats' cost argument. A Warmington win would put the programme's future in doubt.

Flooding.title: New Jersey: Flooding (Fed)
Flooding.subtitle: Flood resilience funding and FEMA's future

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: Flash floods and coastal storms repeatedly hit New Jersey, which relies on federal money to prepare and recover. The Trump administration's push to shrink FEMA's role puts that support in question.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: FEMA cancelled the BRIC resilience programme in April 2025, putting more than $180 million for 35 New Jersey projects at risk, including $20 million to protect an Ocean City sewage plant. A judge ruled the cancellation unlawful, and FEMA now offers up to $1 billion in new BRIC grants. In July 2025 flash floods killed two people in Plainfield. FEMA also denied disaster aid for a February 2026 storm that killed 12.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Trump administration. Its FEMA Review Council says states "should shoulder more of the cost" and proposes moving federal flood insurance policies to the private market.

Democrats. Senators Andy Kim and Cory Booker led the delegation's appeal, saying the request "far exceeds all Stafford Act statutory and regulatory thresholds."

Local leaders. Highlands Mayor Carolyn Broullon is "cautiously optimistic" her town's $12 million flood control grant will arrive.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: Flood aid matters most in shore and river towns, including Jeff Van Drew's 2nd District, rated safely Republican. Booker faces Republican Justin Murphy in a race rated Solid or Safe Democratic.

Infrastructure.title: New Jersey: Infrastructure (State)
Infrastructure.subtitle: Paying for NJ Transit and the power grid

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: Beyond Gateway, New Jersey must fund its own transit system and an overstretched power grid. Both strain the state budget and household bills, and Governor Sherrill has made them early priorities.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: NJ Transit adopted a $3.5 billion operating budget for 2027, with fares covering only 28% of operating revenue and $782 million in capital from the state Transportation Trust Fund. The state is moving about $140 million from the Clean Energy Fund to cover NJ Transit utility costs. Electricity prices rose roughly 20% in June 2025 after regional capacity auctions, with another round of increases due in June 2026.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Democrats. Sherrill declared a utility cost emergency, ordering bill credits and faster solar, storage and gas plant upgrades to "massively expand New Jersey's power generation." NJ Transit's chief cites her "unprecedented level of state funding support."

Republicans. Kean backs a one seat ride on the Raritan Valley Line and NJ Transit's grant bid for the Hunter Flyover in Newark.

Critics. Using clean energy money for transit draws criticism that it departs from the fund's original purpose.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: Infrastructure costs test Sherrill's first year and feed into House races. Raritan Valley riders still transfer in Newark at peak times, a grievance Bennett raises against Kean.

Representation.title: New Jersey: Representation (Fed)
Representation.subtitle: Census counts, redistricting and House seats

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: New Jersey's voice in the House depends on two federal fights, over who is counted in the census and how districts are drawn. Both have intensified in 2026.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: President Trump has ordered work on a census that excludes undocumented immigrants, of whom New Jersey has about 490,000. Missouri has sued to exclude them from the 2030 count, and the administration wants a citizenship question in 2030 field tests. On current trends, the Brennan Center projects New Jersey keeps its 12 seats after 2030. In April 2026 the Supreme Court's Louisiana v. Callais ruling narrowed the Voting Rights Act.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Democrats. Sherrill says New Jersey will "stand up" as a counterbalance. Senate President Nick Scutari backs a mid decade redraw for 2028, which requires voters to amend the state constitution.

Republicans. President Trump and Speaker Mike Johnson cited Callais in urging Republican states to redraw maps before November.

Legal experts. The Constitution counts "the whole number of persons in each State," and Congress, not the President, controls the census.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: The current commission map gave Democrats nine of 12 seats. Any New Jersey redraw would come after 2026, so this November, led by the 7th District, decides whether Republicans keep their three seats under existing lines.

Transit.title: New Jersey: Transit (Fed)
Transit.subtitle: Gateway tunnel funding and commuter rail

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: The $16 billion Gateway project will add new rail tunnels under the Hudson River, a lifeline for New Jersey commuters into New York. The Trump administration's freeze of its funding turned a long planned project into a midterm fight.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: The administration froze Gateway funding in September 2025. Budget director Russ Vought cited "DEI principles," while President Trump called it punishment during the shutdown. A judge ruled on 29 June 2026 that the freeze "flagrantly" broke the law, and the administration dropped its appeal in September. The 7th and 11th Districts hold nearly 60 NJ Transit stations.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Democrats. Governor Mikie Sherrill called the outcome "a big victory for millions of New Jersey commuters." Challenger Rebecca Bennett says Representative Tom Kean Jr. "has been unable to do anything" to secure the money.

Republicans. Kean vows to "counter anybody who gets in my way, including this president," and says he is "leading the fight in Congress" for Gateway. He did not sign a January Democratic letter urging release of the funds.

Labour. The Amalgamated Transit Union and the SMART rail workers' union endorsed Bennett.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: Gateway is the clearest local test of Kean's distance from President Trump. Bennett led 47% to 42% in a September StimSight poll, and most forecasters now rate the 7th District Lean or Likely Democratic.

Energy.title: New Mexico: Energy (Fed)
Energy.subtitle: Federal oil and gas policy and state revenue

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: New Mexico is the nation's second largest oil producer, and much of its output comes from federal land in the Permian Basin. Federal leasing and royalty decisions shape both jobs and the state budget.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: Oil output roughly doubled under President Biden to 2.1 million barrels a day and reached 2.3 million in March 2026. Oil and gas taxes and royalties can supply 25% to 30% of general fund revenue. The 2025 federal law let the Trump administration cut the minimum royalty on new leases to 12.5% from nearly 17%; advocates say one recent sale alone cost residents over $110 million. State land charges 25%.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Republicans. Hull has vowed to "unleash oil and gas" and streamline permits, warning that weakening the industry "puts everybody on edge."

Democrats. Haaland, who paused federal leasing as Interior Secretary, now wants extractive industries to move toward cleaner operations without attacking production. Vasquez blames the Iran war for soaring fuel prices.

Senate. Write in Republican Larry Marker, an oil businessman, backs the industry, while Luján stresses plugging abandoned wells on federal land.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: Oil money funds programmes such as universal childcare, and Haaland is not directly attacking the industry on the trail. Hull leads in the east, but Haaland led 49% to 42% statewide in October.

Health.title: New Mexico: Health (Fed)
Health.subtitle: Medicaid cuts in the most Medicaid reliant state

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: New Mexico has the nation's highest per capita Medicaid enrolment, so federal cuts under H.R. 1 land harder here than almost anywhere. The next governor must decide how far state wealth can fill the gap.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: Medicaid covers about 808,759 New Mexicans, roughly 38% of the population, and the state projects an $8.5 billion loss in federal provider payments from 2028 to 2037. Officials expect about 89,000 to lose coverage under work requirements, possibly over 100,000 with six month eligibility checks. Holy Cross Medical Center in Taos already loses about $2.5 million a year.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Democrats. Deb Haaland would "work toward" a public option and keep covering premium credits Washington cut, calling Medicaid "the surest way" for at risk communities to get care. Representative Gabe Vasquez says over 80,000 face losing care "because of HR1."

Republicans. Gregg Hull wants the state more self sufficient, possibly using its $76 billion sovereign wealth fund, and vows to "fight for every resource."

Senate. Ben Ray Luján, facing only a write in Republican, says Trump's policies leave families "sicker" and poorer.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: Health cuts lead the Democratic message in the swing 2nd District, where a KOB poll showed Vasquez ahead 46% to 43% over Republican Greg Cunningham. Statewide, Haaland led Hull 49% to 42% in October.

Land.title: New Mexico: Land (Fed)
Land.subtitle: Public lands, Chaco and federal protections

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: Federal agencies manage large parts of New Mexico, and the Trump administration is rolling back protections on several of them. The disputes pit drilling and mining against tribal heritage and conservation.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: The Bureau of Land Management is preparing to end a drilling ban around Chaco Culture National Historical Park, a withdrawal covering more than 336,000 acres. Officials also announced reversing a mining ban in the Upper Pecos headwaters, and a Canadian firm has proposed uranium mining near Canjilon in the Carson National Forest. Congressional Republicans failed in 2025 to sell or privatise millions of acres.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Democrats. Senator Martin Heinrich says the administration is "stripping those protections away" to help drilling. Representative Teresa Leger Fernández calls it "an attack on our heritage."

Tribes. The Pueblo of Acoma filed over 400 comments opposing the change, and an Acoma leader calls Chaco "a living cultural landscape."

Republicans. Interior says its review "allows the public to help identify the issues," and write in Senate candidate Larry Marker wants to rebuild mining.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: Public lands help Vasquez, who has denounced Republican land sale efforts, in the swing 2nd District. Haaland carries her record of championing conservation as Interior Secretary into a governor's race she leads by seven points.

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: Nevada hosts the only site where the United States could resume explosive nuclear testing, and Yucca Mountain remains the legal site for national nuclear waste.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: The Nevada National Security Site hosted 100 atmospheric and 828 underground tests from 1951 to 1992. In October 2025 President Trump said the process of resuming testing would "begin immediately." Energy Secretary Chris Wright later said the U.S. would run system tests and "noncritical explosions" instead. On waste, Wright told Congress in April 2026 that "President Trump is not in support of Yucca mountain".

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Democrats. Senators Catherine Cortez Masto and Jacky Rosen back the No Nuclear Testing Without Approval Act, requiring congressional consent for any test. Rosen warns "what happens in Nevada won't just stay in Nevada."

Republicans. Governor Joe Lombardo's office has said he does not support nuclear testing in Nevada. In the 4th District, Republican Cody Whipple says "I don't want Nevada to be a dump" but backs nuclear recycling and science at Yucca.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: Aaron Ford's campaign works to tie Lombardo to President Trump in a toss up race. Emerson put Ford ahead 44% to 42% in September, while Noble Predictive had Lombardo up 2. Whipple faces Democrat Steven Horsford, expected to carry the House testing bill.

Farms.title: New York: Farms (State)
Farms.subtitle: Farm labour costs, overtime and federal pressures

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: Upstate New York's farms, led by dairy, face rising labour costs set in Albany and trade and immigration pressures from Washington. State policy on overtime is the part voters can most directly change.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: New York has 30,650 farms employing over 56,000 people. The farmworker overtime threshold fell to 52 hours a week in 2026 and drops four hours every other year until it reaches 40 in 2032. A state tax credit partly repays farms' overtime costs. The USDA expects milk prices to drop about 10% in 2026, and the state's agriculture commissioner once estimated up to half the farm workforce was undocumented.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Democrats. Hochul's administration adopted the overtime phase in alongside a tax credit, which lawmakers later fixed so all farms qualify. Comptroller Thomas DiNapoli warns of "real concern in rural New York about federal cuts, tariffs and labor shortages."

Farmers. The Farm Bureau opposed the 40 hour threshold, saying it "will change the face of New York agriculture." A Washington County dairy owner calls labour "our number two cost."

Researchers. Cornell's Richard Stup expects workers to "get somewhat less hours in New York."

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: Farm costs matter most upstate, in a race where independents favour Blakeman 44% to 39% even as Hochul leads statewide by nine points. Farm owners say thinner margins are expected in 2026.

Flooding.title: New York: Flooding (Fed)
Flooding.subtitle: Flash flood resilience and FEMA support

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: Flash floods now threaten New York City subways and Hudson Valley towns alike. Resilience projects rely on federal grants, and the Trump administration's push to shrink FEMA has put that money in doubt.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: In 2025 FEMA rescinded $351 million in BRIC grants for New York, mostly city projects such as $50 million cloudburst systems in Central Harlem and East Elmhurst. After a court ruled the cut unlawful, FEMA reopened the programme with up to $1 billion nationally. In September 2026 FEMA sent nearly $117 million to New York and New Jersey for older storm repairs. After the 2023 Hudson Valley floods, FEMA denied individual aid to homeowners.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Trump administration. Its FEMA Review Council says states "should shoulder more of the cost" and proposes moving flood insurance to the private market.

Democrats. Attorney General Letitia James said the cuts "puts millions of New Yorkers at risk."

Local leaders. After the 2023 denial, Orange County's executive noted state aid helped only 57 of more than 900 homeowners who sought help.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: Flood aid matters in Hudson Valley districts such as the 17th, where Lawler faces Conley, and in city seats. Shifting disaster costs to states would also test the next governor's budget.

Healthcare.title: New York: Healthcare (Fed)
Healthcare.subtitle: Federal cuts to the Essential Plan and Medicaid

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: New York built one of the country's broadest public coverage systems with federal money. H.R. 1 pulls much of that money back, forcing the state to choose who keeps coverage and which hospitals survive.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: About 450,000 New Yorkers lost low or no cost Essential Plan coverage in July 2026, mostly people earning above 200% of the poverty line. Hochul warned up to 2 million could lose coverage, about 730,000 from the Essential Plan and 1.3 million from Medicaid, and hospital groups project losses could reach $10 billion a year by 2033. Researchers list 45 to 70 hospitals at risk of closing.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Democrats. Hochul says, "No state can fully undo the damage in this bill." Representative Grace Meng says Blakeman's stance "should disqualify him" from high office.

Republicans. Blakeman promises to eliminate "fraud, waste, and abuse in Medicaid" with a review team, and has said he would "cut Medicaid in half." Representative Mike Lawler says the law "strengthened Medicaid" by removing ineligible people.

Hospitals. Ellenville's hospital chief warns, "There's just not a lot of margin for error."

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: Health cuts are central in Hudson Valley and Long Island seats. Lawler faces Army veteran Cait Conley, the only New York challenger in the DCCC's Red to Blue programme, in the 17th District.

Medicare.title: New York: Medicare (Fed)
Medicare.subtitle: Medicare drug plan premiums for seniors

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: Seniors vote at high rates, and Medicare costs are a federal decision. The Trump administration's end to a drug premium subsidy has given New York Democrats a fresh line of attack on federal health policy.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services is ending the Part D Premium Stabilization Demonstration on 31 December 2026. The temporary programme paid insurers to cap spikes in drug plan premiums. Hochul says about 1.3 million New York seniors will be affected. CMS says that for most beneficiaries premiums will fall, stay the same or rise by less than $10, and that affected enrollees will have at least three plans at $50 a month or less.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Democrats. Hochul calls it "a new assault on seniors" and warns "your monthly premiums will go up." Senator Kirsten Gillibrand calls it "a disaster for seniors."

Trump administration. CMS says "the Part D market is stabilizing" after the Inflation Reduction Act redesign.

State lawmakers. State Senator Gustavo Rivera says he is "appalled" by the decision.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: Premium changes land in early 2027, after the vote, so the fight is over expectations. Swing suburban seats such as Nick LaLota's 1st District, rated Lean to Solid Republican, and Tom Suozzi's Lean Democratic 3rd, are where Medicare messaging matters most.

Transit.title: New York: Transit (Mixed)
Transit.subtitle: Congestion pricing, MTA funding and federal freezes

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: New York's transit system depends on state funding and on federal approvals and grants. The Trump administration's moves against congestion pricing and frozen project money have made the MTA a state and federal battleground.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: Congestion pricing raised $550 million in its first year and cut traffic entering the zone by 11%. Judge Lewis Liman ruled in March 2026 that Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy's bid to end it was "arbitrary and capricious"; the administration appealed in May. Washington also stopped paying its share of the Second Avenue Subway extension in October 2025. In Albany, Governor Kathy Hochul signed a $68.4 billion MTA capital plan, funded partly by a higher payroll tax on large employers.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Democrats. Hochul defends the toll and the capital plan. The MTA's lawyer says, "Secretary Duffy has already lost in court, and if he wants to see us there again, let's go."

Republicans. Bruce Blakeman calls congestion pricing "a tax on the middle class", vows to end it and says "The problem with the MTA is the leadership of the MTA."

Trump administration. The Transportation Department says it "will not stop fighting" to make life more affordable.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: Transit divides the city from suburban drivers. Siena shows Hochul ahead 50% to 41% but only narrowly ahead in the suburbs, 48% to 46%.

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: Ohio voters wrote abortion rights into the state constitution in 2023. Courts and the legislature are still fighting over what limits remain lawful, and the next governor will shape that fight.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: Nearly 58% of voters approved Issue 1 in November 2023. A Franklin County court has paused the state's existing 24 hour waiting period while litigation over the amendment continues. In March 2026 the House passed a new waiting period bill 64 to 32 on a party line vote.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Republicans. Ramaswamy calls himself unapologetically pro life and has said he would support a ban at six weeks.

Democrats. Acton says every Ohioan deserves the right to make their own reproductive health decisions.

Voters. Planned Parenthood's Ohio advocates call retreading rejected legislation reprehensible.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: A governor cannot override the constitution, but can sign or veto new restrictions that test it in court. Abortion helps Acton with suburban women and independents, and lets her frame the race as a choice about protecting a result voters already chose. Ramaswamy's past remarks give Democrats a clear contrast in a race where Acton holds a small lead in most polls.

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: The February 2023 Norfolk Southern derailment in East Palestine released toxic chemicals and shook faith in rail safety. Federal rail reform remains unfinished, and both Senate candidates claim the cause.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: Payments from a $600 million class settlement began flowing in 2026 after the Supreme Court denied objections. The reintroduced Railway Safety Act would raise penalties from $100,000 to $10 million and require two person crews. In May, President Trump urged Congress to pass it.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Republicans. Senator Jon Husted cosponsors the 2026 bill alongside Democrats such as Maria Cantwell, calling it a balanced, data driven approach that supports the freight rail industry.

Democrats. Sherrod Brown introduced the original bill with J.D. Vance in 2023, though it never passed.

Voters. Some people outside the class say payouts are too small and ignore future harms.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: Rail safety lets Brown remind voters of his record and lets Husted show independence from the rail industry. East Palestine sits in a Republican leaning corner of eastern Ohio, so the issue could help Brown with voters who usually back Republicans. With both men backing reform, the question is who can get it passed. Brown leads Husted 49% to 43% in the CNN poll.

Tariffs.title: Ohio: Tariffs (Fed)
Tariffs.subtitle: Trade policy and the auto supply chain

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: Ohio's auto plants and farms are exposed to President Trump's tariffs, especially in the trade war with Canada. Tariffs have become a core affordability issue in the Senate race.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: A taxpayer group estimates tariffs have cost Ohio about $11 billion since January 2025, or roughly $2,274 per household, ranking it ninth nationally. Auto parts are the most affected import, with $1.5 billion in tariffs. After the Supreme Court ruling, GM expected a $500 million refund, worth about $500 to each UAW member through profit sharing.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Democrats. Brown says ending the war and the tariffs would quickly lower gas, diesel and food costs.

Republicans. Husted wants a deal to end the trade war with Canada and has said he is typically not in favour of a tax or tariff.

Voters. A Cato Institute survey found three quarters of Americans say tariffs raised prices.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: Husted's distance from the President on tariffs shows how costly the issue is for Republicans. Union members make up 12% of Ohio's workforce, a group Brown has long courted. The race is close in most polls, so blue collar voters may decide it.

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: Rising property taxes have sparked a voter revolt in Ohio, including a push to abolish them entirely. Tax relief is a central pledge for both candidates for governor, Vivek Ramaswamy and Amy Acton.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: A campaign to abolish property taxes, which provide nearly two thirds of local revenue, missed the November ballot and now aims for 2027. Opponents say it would wipe out more than $21 billion in local funding. The Tax Foundation put the cost of total elimination at $20 billion a year.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Republicans. Ramaswamy wants to roll property taxes back to levels before the pandemic and cap growth, and to make Ohio a zero income tax state.

Democrats. Acton says property taxes rise because the statehouse underfunds schools, and proposes more state school aid and a larger homestead exemption.

Voters. Governor Mike DeWine warned total elimination would be devastating for police, fire and schools.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: Ramaswamy has softened from abolition to a rollback, a sign of the issue's risks. Acton ties taxes to school funding, which plays well in suburbs. She leads 50% to 42% in the CNN poll, though polls range from a two point Ramaswamy lead to an eight point Acton lead.

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: Toxic algal blooms fed by farm runoff threaten Lake Erie, a drinking water source for millions. Protection depends on state programmes such as H2Ohio and on federal monitoring, both under financial pressure.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: Ohio, Michigan and Ontario agreed to cut phosphorus entering the lake 40% by 2025 but missed the goal, and NOAA forecast a moderate bloom for 2026. The legislature cut H2Ohio funding by 39%, more than $50 million. Federal staffing cuts paused NOAA toxin monitoring devices, and 11 million people rely on the lake for drinking water.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Democrats. Acton opposes loosening air and water standards for data centres.

Republicans. Ramaswamy wants data centres to cover their own energy and water costs.

Voters. The Alliance for the Great Lakes says Ohio must get more aggressive after missing the 2025 target.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: Water matters most around Toledo and the lake's western basin. Budget cuts give Acton an argument about priorities, while Republicans point to voluntary farm programmes that pay growers to cut runoff. Missing the 2025 phosphorus target weakens the case that voluntary measures are enough. The issue also overlaps with the growing data centre debate in both races.

Ethics.title: Pennsylvania: Ethics (Fed)
Ethics.subtitle: Congressional stock trading and the 8th District

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: Congressional stock trading has become a defining issue in northeastern Pennsylvania. Representative Rob Bresnahan's trades turned a national reform debate into a local test of trust.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: Bresnahan made almost 650 stock trades in 2025, including dozens around the "Liberation Day" tariff announcement. He sold up to $130,000 in shares of four companies that run about half of Medicaid managed care plans shortly before voting for H.R. 1. He says an adviser made the trades and that he has stopped trading. The House passed a Stop Insider Trading Act 232 to 198, but it failed in the Senate on 30 September.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Republicans. Bresnahan backs a ban, saying "Members of Congress should never be allowed to trade their own stocks," and introduced his own bill in May 2025.

Democrats. Scranton Mayor Paige Cognetti says "No one should be able to use their public office to enrich themselves," and wants a permanent lobbying ban for former members.

Voters. A Franklin and Marshall poll found voters rank government and politicians among the state's most important problems.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: The Cook Political Report rates the 8th District a toss up. Bresnahan flipped it in 2024 with 50.8%, and Quinnipiac finds 54% of Pennsylvania voters want Democrats to control the House.

Immigration.title: Pennsylvania: Immigration (Fed)
Immigration.subtitle: ICE arrests, detention plans and local cooperation

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: Federal immigration enforcement has grown sharply in Pennsylvania, testing how far the state will cooperate. The governor's race offers a clear contrast on working with ICE.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: Arrests followed by detention rose from 276 in January 2025 to 1,150 in July 2026. Some 140 local governments hold 287(g) partnerships with ICE, the fourth most in the country. ICE bought warehouses in Berks and Schuylkill counties to convert into detention centres, but abandoned the plans after state environmental orders cut off water and sewage. An AP analysis found ICE arrests in the state more than quadrupled compared with the end of the Biden years.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Democrats. Shapiro says, "We do not do ICE's work for them here in Pennsylvania," and vowed to use "every tool" against the detention warehouses.

Republicans. Garrity says officials should "cooperate" with ICE and called Shapiro's opposition "posturing." Her campaign wants a governor "who will work with the federal government, not sue it."

Farms. About 7.5% of workers hired by Pennsylvania farms in 2022 were migrants.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: Shapiro leads Garrity by about 25 points, with President Trump's approval at 37%. Immigration matters more in swing House seats such as the 7th and the 1st, where Brian Fitzpatrick narrowly leads Bob Harvie in Democratic polls.

Logistics.title: Pennsylvania: Logistics (State)
Logistics.subtitle: Warehouse growth, local control and truck traffic

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: Eastern Pennsylvania became a national warehouse hub, bringing jobs but also truck traffic and land fights. State law decides how much say towns have, and lawmakers remain split.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: The Lehigh Valley delivered 32 million square feet of warehouse space from 2020 to mid 2025, and supply has grown 44% since 2017. The building pipeline has since shrunk sharply and vacancy reached 8.8%. Trade, transportation and utilities jobs were around 92,000 locally in 2022, the region's largest sector.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Democrats. Representative Mike Schlossberg's HB 782 would require detailed traffic, pollution and safety studies for major projects, though he says "I don't want to stop warehouses."

Republicans. Representative Joe Emrick's HB 1960 would require a local referendum for large warehouses, so "the community can say with one voice" how growth continues.

Business. Economic developers cite Shapiro's push to "streamline permitting and move at the speed of business" and warn studies would hurt competitiveness.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: Warehouses shape the Lehigh Valley's 7th District, where Republican Ryan Mackenzie faces Democrat Bob Brooks in a race rated a toss up. A Democratic poll had Brooks ahead 47% to 43%.

Nuclear.title: Pennsylvania: Nuclear (Fed)
Nuclear.subtitle: Reactor restarts, data centres and federal support

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: Pennsylvania is at the centre of a nuclear revival driven by data centre demand. Federal loans, licensing and deals with reactor maker Westinghouse shape how fast it happens and who benefits.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: The Energy Department closed a $1 billion loan to restart the Three Mile Island reactor, expected online in 2027 to power Microsoft data centres. Talen will supply Amazon with 1,920 megawatts from the Susquehanna plant through 2042. The Commerce Department's tentative deal with Pennsylvania based Westinghouse targets at least $80 billion in new reactors, with the government taking a share of future profits.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Trump administration. Energy Secretary Chris Wright says the restart "will provide affordable, reliable, and secure energy."

Democrats. Governor Josh Shapiro filed a federal complaint over PJM's slow grid connections and negotiated a cap on capacity prices.

Republicans. Stacy Garrity focuses on natural gas, promising to "fast track permits" for gas, pipelines and power plants, and wants data centres kept to brownfield and industrial sites.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: Nuclear power wins support for jobs, but its data centre link is a liability. Quinnipiac finds 64% of voters say AI data centres do more harm than good, while Shapiro leads Garrity by about 25 points.

Border.title: Texas: Border (Fed)
Border.subtitle: Border security after the crossing collapse

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: Border security has defined Texas politics for a decade. With crossings far lower, the debate now turns on federal money, state enforcement and how immigration is handled once people are inside the country.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: Washington awarded Texas $7.5 billion in September 2026 to repay border costs; the state says it spent over $10 billion during the Biden years. Apprehensions continue at lower levels, including more than 1,700 in the Rio Grande Valley and Coastal Bend counties in March 2026.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Republicans. Senate nominee Ken Paxton led lawsuits against the Biden administration over razor wire and Shelby Park, backed Senate Bill 4 and is endorsed by the National Border Patrol Council. Governor Greg Abbott says "Texas held the line when Washington would not."

Democrats. James Talarico wants "a lock on the door and a welcome mat out front," with more resources at ports of entry and an ICE overhaul focused on criminals. He voted against Senate Bill 4.

Voters. Talarico leads Paxton among Latino voters 54% to 41%.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: The border no longer guarantees Republican dominance. The Texas Politics Project shows Talarico ahead 50% to 47%, and Democrat Gina Hinojosa at 49% to Abbott's 48%, both within the margin of error.

Ethics.title: Texas: Ethics (Fed)
Ethics.subtitle: Paxton's record, a pardon and a House scandal

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: Ethics questions run through Texas's federal races, from the Senate nominee to House seats. Each party now has a figure the other can point to.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: Paxton was impeached by the Texas House in 2023 and acquitted by the Senate on all 16 articles. A securities fraud case ended in a 2024 pretrial deal, and four fired deputies won $6.6 million in a whistleblower suit. President Trump pardoned Representative Henry Cuellar and his wife in a foreign bribery case. Republican Tony Gonzales dropped his reelection bid amid a House Ethics inquiry into an affair with a staffer.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Democrats. Talarico calls Paxton "The Most Corrupt Politician in America"; his campaign says Paxton "became a multimillionaire on a government salary."

Republicans. Paxton says voters care about "what have you done for them" and calls Talarico the "most extreme radical the Democrats have ever nominated."

Trump. After the pardon, he criticised Cuellar's "lack of LOYALTY" for staying a Democrat.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: Paxton beat Senator John Cornyn in the May runoff, and ethics is now the core Democratic case against him. Talarico leads 50% to 47% and wins independents 69% to 11%.

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: Texas' Affordable Care Act marketplace grew from about 1.3 million enrollees in 2021 to nearly 4 million in 2025, so the expiry of enhanced federal subsidies hit it hard. Healthcare costs are a sharp contrast in the Senate race.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: Texas marketplace enrolment fell 4% to 3.28 million in 2026, its first annual drop since 2019. The average monthly premium per person rose from $57 to $89 after subsidies lapsed, and only 79% of enrollees paid their first premium, leaving nearly 900,000 without effective coverage. A Senate bill to extend the credits won four Republicans but fell short of 60 votes.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Democrats. Talarico backs a Medicare buy in for all ages, protection for existing conditions and Medicaid expansion in Texas. He cites a $684 insulin bill after his diabetes diagnosis.

Republicans. Paxton favours tax deductions of $25,000 for medical costs, has fought to overturn the ACA and won settlements from drug companies as attorney general.

Insurers. Bronze plan selections rose from 18% to 31%, as buyers traded down to cheaper coverage.

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: Healthcare helps Talarico with suburban voters, whom he leads 54% to 44%. Women back him 56% to 40%.

Tariffs.title: Texas: Tariffs (Fed)
Tariffs.subtitle: Tariffs, USMCA and trade with Mexico

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: Texas is the gateway for trade with Mexico, so federal tariff and trade decisions hit its border cities, farms and factories directly.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: Port Laredo handled over $354 billion in trade in 2025, the busiest inland port on the border. The Supreme Court struck down President Trump's emergency "reciprocal" tariffs in February 2026, but Section 232 duties on steel, aluminum and auto parts remain, and the President announced a 10% global tariff in response. At the July 2026 joint review, the U.S. declined to extend USMCA, triggering annual reviews; the pact stays in force until 2036 unless renewed.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Business. The South Texas Manufacturers Association says steel and aluminum tariffs raise costs and domestic producers raise prices "to mask the tariffs."

Farmers. A Corpus Christi grower says the region depends on Mexican trade and the "peso value as well as the dollar." U.S. farm exports to Mexico reached $30.6 billion in 2025.

Local leaders. San Antonio Mayor Gina Ortiz Jones says a trade deal "absent an ability to actually execute it, doesn't do anyone any good."

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: Trade uncertainty weighs on South Texas, where Cuellar and other border Democrats defend seats. Statewide, voters favour Republicans on the generic House ballot 47% to 42%, even as Democrats lead the top races.

Wind.title: Virginia: Wind (Fed)
Wind.subtitle: Coastal Virginia Offshore Wind and federal opposition

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: Off Virginia Beach, Dominion is building the largest offshore wind project in the country. President Trump's hostility to wind has put a project backed by both parties in Hampton Roads at risk.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: Coastal Virginia Offshore Wind will have 176 turbines and 2.6 gigawatts, enough for 660,000 homes, at a cost of $11.2 billion, with completion expected by the end of 2026. The Interior Department issued a 90 day stop order on national security grounds, but a federal judge allowed work to resume about three weeks later. President Trump has said, "We're not allowing any windmills to go up."

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Republicans. Representative Jen Kiggans backs the project for jobs and grid upgrades serving Naval Air Station Oceana, and joined House Republicans opposing the pause. Speaker Mike Johnson said "we want to do right by" Virginians.

Democrats. Challenger Elaine Luria, who founded the Offshore Wind Caucus, says Kiggans' efforts "did nothing." The state's Democratic delegation called the ruling "a victory for Virginians."

Ratepayers. Attorney General Jay Jones says his office will "protect ratepayers."

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: Wind is a defining issue in the 2nd District rematch, rated Likely Democratic to toss up. A Democratic poll showed Kiggans and Luria tied at 47%.

Workforce.title: Virginia: Workforce (Fed)
Workforce.subtitle: Federal job cuts and Virginia's economy

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: Virginia is home to about 350,000 civilian federal employees, more than half in Northern Virginia. The Trump administration's cuts to the federal workforce have reshaped the state's job market and its federal races.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: Virginia lost a net 23,500 civilian federal jobs through November 2025, wiping out six years of gains in 11 months. One economist says that equals losing 47,000 private sector jobs. Governor Abigail Spanberger reported a loss of 43,600 jobs, mainly in federal and professional services, in fiscal 2026. Hampton Roads lost about 6,300 federal jobs in 2025, a 10.5% drop.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
Democrats. Senator Mark Warner says he wishes he had done more to prevent the cuts, but cautions against simply restoring old staffing levels. Spanberger blames DOGE's "slashing of our federal workforce."

Republicans. Warner's challenger, retired Army Major General Bert Mizusawa, argues for change and more domestic energy production.

Economists. UVA's Eric Scorsone says "Virginia has really relied on the federal government."

sections.heading: Electoral Impact
sections.html: Federal job losses matter most in the 1st and 7th Districts. Rob Wittman faces Democrat Shannon Taylor in a seat rated Likely Republican to toss up, and Eugene Vindman is favoured in the 7th. Courts voided Virginia's redistricting vote, so 2021 lines stay.

Pricing.title: Washington: Pricing (Fed)
Pricing.subtitle: Federal power rates and fuel prices

sections.heading: Issue Overview
sections.html: Washington households face record fuel prices and rising electricity costs. The federal Bonneville Power Administration sells power to more than 300 Northwest utilities, so decisions in Washington, D.C. shape bills directly.

sections.heading: Key Data & Trends
sections.html: BPA, which owns about 75% of the region's transmission lines, has proposed a 6.3% rate increase to cover a $250 million shortfall, tied partly to court ordered salmon spill after the Trump administration left a 2023 agreement. Earthjustice says BPA's choice of the Markets+ power market could cost customers $165 million to $221 million a year more than the alternative. Washington gas averaged $5.79 a gallon in May 2026, against $4.56 nationally.

sections.heading: Partisan Stances
sections.html:
